1017365272404305|d2d4.headline: Take the free pawn with 3.Nxe5; 3.d4 lets Black swap it
1017365272404305|d2d4.why: 2...Bc5 leaves the e5 pawn with no defender. 3.d4 lets Black trade it off with 3...exd4, and after 4.Bc4 d6 5.Nxd4 material is level and so is the game. 3.Nxe5 takes it: the theory calls this gambit unsound, because if 3...Qh4, threatening mate on f2 and hitting the knight, 4.Qe2 meets both threats. In the engine line 3...Nc6 4.Nxc6 dxc6 turns it into a Stafford gambit and you stay a pawn up with a clear advantage.
1017365272404305|d2d4.principle: Start with captures, then check your opponent's forcing replies: here the e5 pawn is free, and the only scary answer, ...Qh4, is met by Qe2.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Bc5

1017365272404305|f1c4.headline: Take the free e5 pawn: the Busch-Gass gambit is unsound
1017365272404305|f1c4.why: 2...Bc5 leaves the e5 pawn with no defender, which hands White a clear advantage. 3.Bc4 throws that away by giving Black time for 3...Nc6 or 3...d6, and the game is level again. Take it with 3.Nxe5: Black's idea is 3...Qh4, hitting f2 and the knight, but 4.Qe2 meets both threats, and theory rates the gambit unsound as long as you stay calm.
1017365272404305|f1c4.principle: Accept a gambit pawn when you can meet the threats behind it; declining for safety gives back the advantage the gambit handed you.

1062777786489002|c1b2.headline: The queen on f6 is a target: 8.e5 kicks it
1062777786489002|c1b2.why: 7...Qf6 puts the queen where your e-pawn can hit it. 8.Bb2 is too slow: Black answers 8...d3, and after 9.e5 Qh6 the queen has found a good square and your advantage is gone. 8.e5 claims the centre and attacks the queen at once; after 8...Qd8 she is back home, and 9.Re1 Be7 10.cxd4 wins back a pawn and builds your centre, with a large advantage.
1062777786489002|c1b2.principle: When an enemy piece, especially the queen, stands where one of your pawns can attack it, push the pawn: you gain space and your opponent loses time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4/4...Bxb4/5. c3/5...Bc5

1095756382312296|d1e2.headline: Punish ...g6 with ...e6: 8.Nb5 jumps at the d6 hole
1095756382312296|d1e2.why: With ...g6 and ...e6 both played, no black pawn can ever guard d6, and your bishop on f4 already eyes d6 and c7. 8.Qe2 is too slow: Black closes the hole with 8...a6 and 9...d6, and the chance is gone. 8.Nb5 jumps straight at those squares: after 8...Qa5+ 9.Kf1 Kf8 10.Bc7 b6 11.Bd6+ Black's king is stuck on f8, his pieces are tied up, and White is close to winning. The theory warns that ...g6 combined with ...e6 weakens the dark squares around Black's king and gives the same 8.Nb5 jump as the punishment.
1095756382312296|d1e2.principle: A square the enemy pawns can no longer cover is an outpost: once ...e6 is played, aim your knight and bishop at d6 before Black can plug it with a piece.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Nxc3/4...Nc6/5. Nf3/5...g6

1095756382312296|e1h1.headline: Strike at d6 with 8.Nb5 before Black castles
1095756382312296|e1h1.why: 8.O-O gives Black time for 8...a6 9.Bb3 Nge7 and castling, and almost all of your huge advantage disappears. Theory warns that combining ...g6 with ...e6 badly weakens the dark squares around Black's king, and with your bishop already on f4 the d6 square is a target. 8.Nb5 aims the knight at d6 and c7 together: after 8...Qa5+ 9.Kf1 Kf8 Black has given up castling, and 10.Bc7 b6 11.Bd6+ Nge7 keeps Black's pieces tied up.
1095756382312296|e1h1.principle: With more pieces out and the enemy king uncastled, open lines and strike at once; give Black one quiet move and he castles to safety.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Nxc3/4...Nc6/5. Nf3/5...g6

1102494195291015|f3g5.headline: Recapture on c3 with a new piece, not a lone f7 raid
1102494195291015|f3g5.why: 8.Ng5 moves the knight a second time with two minor pieces still at home, and 8...Ne5 covers f7: after 9.Nxf7 Nxf7 10.Bxf7+ Kxf7 you have given a knight for a pawn and Black is better. Black's 7...dxc3 grabbed another pawn instead of developing, and the pawn on c3 is attacked once and not defended at all. 8.Nxc3 wins it back while developing toward the centre, and Black is so far behind that the engine's line has 8...Kf8, giving up castling, while you keep a big advantage.
1102494195291015|f3g5.principle: In a gambit you have paid pawns for a lead in development, so each move should bring another piece into the game, not send an already developed knight on a raid that can be parried.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4/4...Bxb4/5. c3/5...Bd6

1110098787406126|c1e3.headline: 6.f3 starts a pawn chase against the bishop and the e6 queen
1110098787406126|c1e3.why: 6.Be3 develops, but it lets Black trade bishops with 6...Bxe2 7.Qxe2 and settle with ...Nf6, ...c6 and ...Nd5; your edge shrinks. As the theory notes say, the early queen checks achieve little and Black's queen blocks the e-pawn. 6.f3 attacks the bishop on g4, and after 6...Bf5 7.g4 Bg6 8.f4 your pawns gain space with tempo, since a pawn on f5 would hit both the queen on e6 and the bishop on g6; Black has to stop it with 8...f5, and White keeps a large advantage.
1110098787406126|c1e3.principle: When the opponent's bishop and early queen stand where your pawns can reach them, advance the pawns with tempo: you gain space and they lose time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3

1206106476480095|d5e6.headline: Keep queens on: 9.Bxc6 wins another pawn against an exposed king
1206106476480095|d5e6.why: 9.Bxe6+ Kxe6 10.Qh3+ Qf5 11.Qxf5+ Kxf5 trades queens, and without them Black's wandering king is no longer in danger, so a good part of your advantage evaporates. 9.Bxc6 removes the knight instead: after 9...bxc6 10.Qxc6 you win a pawn, your queen hits the bishop on e6 and the rook in the corner, and Black's queenside pawns are broken. With queens still on the board and Black's king on f7, you keep a big attacking advantage.
1206106476480095|d5e6.principle: When you have the attack against an exposed king, keep the queens on and win material with threats; a queen trade lets the advantage fade.

1206106476480095|f3f6.headline: Keep the queens on against the exposed king: 9.Bxc6
1206106476480095|f3f6.why: 9.Qxf6+ trades queens, and after 9...gxf6 10.Bxe6+ Kxe6 Black's king is perfectly safe in an endgame, so most of your advantage evaporates. 9.Bxc6 removes the knight on c6 instead, and after 9...bxc6 10.Qxc6 your queen takes a second pawn with the queens still on the board, against a king that can no longer castle.
1206106476480095|f3f6.principle: Play to your imbalances: your trump is Black's exposed king, so keep the queens on and win material with the minor pieces rather than trading into an endgame.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...d5/5. exd5/5...Nxd5/6. Nxf7/6...Kxf7

1251051945717105|a5c7.headline: Develop with 7...Nf6; the queen can move later
1251051945717105|a5c7.why: 7...Qc7 moves the queen again while all four of your minor pieces are still at home. White uses the time: after 8.d5 Bd7 9.Rc1 your queen faces the rook on c1 with only the c3 knight in between, and after 9...Nf6 10.Nf3 Qd8 she has gone back home while White is clearly better. 7...Nf6 develops the knight toward the centre; in the line 8.Bc4 Nc6 9.Nf3 Be7 10.O-O O-O the queen does go to c7, with 11...Qc7, but only once your pieces are out and your king is safe.
1251051945717105|a5c7.principle: In the opening, every move should develop a piece or fight for the centre; a queen move that does neither must have a concrete reason, and fear of a future attack is not enough.

1261108510304489|e1h1.headline: Two pawns down, aim at f7 with 7.Qb3
1261108510304489|e1h1.why: 7.O-O is too slow when you are two pawns down: 7...Nf6 8.e5 Ne4 9.cxd4 d5 hits your bishop and Black comes out better. 7.Qb3 lines the queen up behind the bishop on c4 against f7, which only the king defends, so Black has to deal with 8.Bxf7+ at once. In the main line 7...Na5 8.Bxf7+ Kf8 9.Qa4 Kxf7 10.Qxa5 you win back a pawn and the game is level.
1261108510304489|e1h1.principle: When f7 is guarded only by the king, a queen and bishop aimed at it make a threat the opponent must answer before anything else.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4/4...Bxb4/5. c3/5...Be7

1314504257002276|f1d3.headline: Close the centre with 3.e5 instead of defending with Bd3
1314504257002276|f1d3.why: The theory notes call 3.Bd3 irregular: after 3...dxe4 4.Bxe4 Nf6 Black develops with tempo on the bishop, which must move again, or be swapped for a knight with 5.Nc3 Nxe4 6.Nxe4, giving up the bishop pair. In the line 5.Bf3 Bf5 Black has easy development and is slightly better. 3.e5, the advance variation and the masters' top choice (39.9%), closes the centre and gains space; after 3...Bf5 4.Nf3 e6 5.Be2 White keeps a small edge. 3.Nc3, 3.Nd2 and 3.exd5 are also good.
1314504257002276|f1d3.principle: Don't put a piece where the opponent can make it move again with tempo; every extra move of the same piece is development your opponent gets for free.

1317312578379376|f3c6.headline: The f6 queen guards c6: keep your queen with 10.Qh5+
1317312578379376|f3c6.why: After the Fried Liver sacrifice you are clearly winning, but 10.Qxc6+ grabs a pawn the queen on f6 defends along the sixth rank: 10...Qxc6 wins your queen and turns the game around. 10.Qh5+ keeps the attack instead: 10...g6 loosens Black's kingside, and 11.Qe2 keeps your queen and the pressure on a king stuck in the centre.
1317312578379376|f3c6.principle: Before any capture, and especially a capture with check, count the defenders of the square, including a queen guarding it from along a rank.

132233271809428|a7a6.headline: Break the pin on c6 with 5...Bd7
132233271809428|a7a6.why: 5.Bb5 pins your knight on c6, and White threatens Bxc6+, which 5...a6 does not prevent: after 6.Bxc6+ bxc6 your c-pawns are doubled, and in the line 7.d3 c4 8.dxc4 you end up a pawn down. 5...Bd7 develops and blocks the pin, so if 6.Bxc6 you recapture with the bishop (6...Bxc6) and keep a sound pawn structure. Then the king's knight comes into play with 7...Nh6 and 8...Nf5, and Black is better.
132233271809428|a7a6.principle: When a bishop pins your knight to the king, block the pin with a developing move so that the exchange on c6 no longer wrecks your pawns.

1364829931449246|c1e3.headline: Keep the queens on with 7.Qd3; your space needs them
1364829931449246|c1e3.why: Black threatens 7...Qxd4, and 7.Be3 only meets it by allowing the queen trade: after 7...Qxd4 8.Bxd4 Ne7 9.Be3 Be6 10.Bxe6 fxe6 the queens and light-squared bishops are gone and your advantage has evaporated. Theory notes that in the Paris Defence Black's kingside bishop is shut in behind the pawn chain while White has more space. 7.Qd3 keeps the queens on so that space counts: after 7...Be7 8.O-O c6 9.Re1 Nh6 10.h3 you are castled, your rook is on the e-file and Black is still untangling.
1364829931449246|c1e3.principle: Your trumps here are space and development; avoid trades that relieve the cramped side and keep the queens on.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...d6

1436063243700465|f6d5.headline: Recapture with the pawn, 4...cxd5, so e4 can't chase your knight
1436063243700465|f6d5.why: 4...Nxd5 puts the knight where a pawn can hit it: 5.e4 Nb6 builds White a full pawn centre with tempo, and after 6.h3 g6 7.Nc3 Bg7 White is clearly better. The pawn on d5 is attacked three times and not defended at all, so you can choose how to take it back. 4...cxd5, played in 99.7% of master games, recaptures toward the centre and keeps a pawn on d5, so White has no e4 with tempo; after 5.Bf4 Nc6 6.Nc3 a6 the game is level.
1436063243700465|f6d5.principle: A knight in the centre that an enemy pawn can attack loses time when it is chased; recapture with a pawn when you can.

1455931362502230|c8f5.headline: After 4.Bf4, c4 is undefended: take it with 4...dxc4
1455931362502230|c8f5.why: 4.Bf4 develops a bishop but leaves c4 attacked once and defended not at all. 4...Bf5 lets that go, and 5.Qb3 attacks b7, which the bishop stopped guarding when it left c8, so White takes over the initiative. Take the pawn with 4...dxc4: the theory says that after 4.Bf4 Black keeps it without White getting compensation, which is why 4.e3, ruling out 4...dxc4, is the normal move.
1455931362502230|c8f5.principle: After each opponent move, check what has become loose: a developing move that leaves the c4 pawn unguarded is a free pawn.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6

1483132126480579|c1d2.headline: Use your lead: 7.e5 keeps the g8 knight off f6
1483132126480579|c1d2.why: 7.Bd2 is a passive square for the bishop, and Black catches up calmly with 7...d6 8.h3 Nf6 9.O-O O-O: your gambit compensation is gone and Black is slightly better. The theory notes recommend 7.e5 (48.5% of masters games): the pawn takes f6 away from Black's knight, and it is not really hanging, because after 7...Nxe5 8.Nxe5 Bxe5 9.Bxf7+ Kxf7 10.Qd5+ Kg7 11.Qxe5+ White wins the piece back. If Black challenges it with 7...d6 8.exd6, the recapture 8...exd6 runs into 9.Nb5.
1483132126480579|c1d2.principle: In a gambit your pawn buys time, so use it: keep the opponent's pieces out of play and open lines before they finish developing, instead of making quiet moves.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Nxc3/4...Nc6/5. Nf3/5...g6

1483132126480579|c1g5.headline: 7.e5 takes f6 from Black's knight; the pawn is tactically defended
1483132126480579|c1g5.why: 7.Bg5 lets Black develop normally with 7...Nf6, and after 8.h3 d6 9.O-O O-O Black has castled and keeps the gambit pawn with a slightly better game. Theory recommends 7.e5: while the pawn stands there, Black's knight cannot develop to f6, and in the engine line it goes to h6 instead. The pawn only looks loose: theory shows 7...Nxe5 8.Nxe5 Bxe5 9.Bxf7+ Kxf7 10.Qd5+ Kg7 11.Qxe5+ wins the piece back with the better game for White.
1483132126480579|c1g5.principle: Ask where your opponent's next developing move wants to go and take that square away, especially when a tactic covers the pawn that does it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Nxc3/4...Nc6/5. Nf3/5...g6

1513949415486855|e4d5.headline: Gain space with 4.e5 instead of releasing the tension
1513949415486855|e4d5.why: 4.exd5 exd5 releases the tension and gives Black an open, symmetrical position with free development, so most of your edge disappears. Black's threat was 4...dxe4, and 4.e5, the main move in 84.2% of master games, meets it by taking space with tempo on the knight on f6, which the theory describes as the main answer to ...Nf6. After 4...Nfd7 Black has to attack your centre with ...c5 and ...Nc6, and you support it with 6.c3 and castle, keeping the extra space.
1513949415486855|e4d5.principle: When you can choose between a space advantage and a symmetrical exchange, keep the imbalance that favours you: the e5 pawn cramps Black, while exd5 leaves nothing to play for.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. d4/2...Nf6

1557996217562153|c2c3.headline: 2...Nc6 lets you gain space with 3.d5
1557996217562153|c2c3.why: Against 2.d4 Black should take with 2...cxd4. 2...Nc6 instead attacks d4 and threatens 3...cxd4, winning a pawn, but it puts the knight where your d-pawn can hit it. 3.c3 defends passively, and after 3...d5 4.exd5 Qxd5 Black is comfortable. 3.d5 attacks the knight and takes space: after 3...Na5 4.Nf3 g6 5.h4 the knight on a5 is offside.
1557996217562153|c2c3.principle: When a knight on c6 attacks your d4 pawn, pushing d5 saves the pawn, gains space and drives the knight to a worse square.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4

1557996217562153|g1f3.headline: Punish 2...Nc6 with 3.d5, kicking the knight
1557996217562153|g1f3.why: The theory says Black should play 2...cxd4; after 2...Nc6, 3.Nf3 lets Black take on d4 anyway, and 3...cxd4 4.Nxd4 is an ordinary open Sicilian in which your big advantage is gone. 3.d5 punishes the move: the pawn steps out of the c5 pawn's reach, gains space and attacks the knight on c6. After 3...Na5 the knight is stuck on the rim, and White keeps a big space advantage and a clear edge.
1557996217562153|g1f3.principle: When a knight lands in front of your centre pawns and a pawn advance can hit it, push: you gain space and the knight loses time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4

15856967415293|c1g5.headline: Castle first with 7.O-O; 7.Bg5 just gets chased around
15856967415293|c1g5.why: 7.Bg5 hits the queen, but 7...Nge7 blocks with a developing move, and then ...h6, ...Ne5 and ...N5g6 chase your bishops while Black castles, leaving Black clearly better. 7.O-O is the main move (58.7% of master games; 7.Qb3 is the other): your king is safe before the centre opens. In the main line 7...Nf6 8.cxd4 Nxe4 9.d5 gains space with tempo on the knight, and 10.Qd4 and 11.Bg5 bring your pieces in with a roughly balanced game.
15856967415293|c1g5.principle: In open gambit positions castle before starting operations; a piece sortie that the opponent meets with gain of time leaves your king in the centre for nothing.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4/4...Bxb4/5. c3/5...Ba5/6. d4

15856967415293|f3g5.headline: Castle with 7.O-O; the lone 7.Ng5 raid is easily parried
15856967415293|f3g5.why: 7.Ng5 moves the knight again to hit f7, but 7...Nh6 covers it, and after 8.O-O dxc3 9.Qb3 O-O 10.Nxc3 Black has castled and you are two pawns down with no attack left. 7.O-O, the top master choice (58.7%), gets your king safe and keeps the gambit's lead in development: after 7...Nf6 8.cxd4 Nxe4 9.d5 Ne7 10.Qd4 you gain time against Black's knights and the game is about level. 7.Qb3 is the other main move.
15856967415293|f3g5.principle: In a gambit your compensation is development, so spend each move bringing a new piece out or castling, not on a one-move threat with a piece that is already out.

1652894211754070|g1f3.headline: 4...Bg6 is unusual: strike with 5.e6 before Black plays ...e6
1652894211754070|g1f3.why: Theory calls 4...Bg6 a highly unusual reply to 4.Bd3: Black avoids the bishop trade but hasn't played ...e6, so the e6 square is still open to your pawn. 5.Nf3 lets Black fix that with 5...e6 and reach a normal Advance structure. 5.e6 strikes first: after 5...Qc8 6.exf7+ Bxf7 Black's king is loosened, and 7.Nf3 Nf6 8.Ne5 hits the bishop on f7, with a clear advantage.
1652894211754070|g1f3.principle: When your opponent spends moves shuffling a bishop, open lines with a pawn break before they finish developing.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. e5/3...Bf5/4. Bd3/4...Bg6

1652894211754070|h2h4.headline: Break with 5.e6 while Black's kingside is undeveloped
1652894211754070|h2h4.why: 5.h4, the usual pawn chase against the g6 bishop, gives Black time to trade it with 5...Bxd3 6.cxd3, leaving you with doubled d-pawns and much of your edge gone. 5.e6 strikes before Black has developed a kingside piece: the pawn hits f7, and after 5...Qc8 6.exf7+ Bxf7 7.Nf3 Nf6 8.Ne5 e6 9.Nxf7 Kxf7 you have the bishop pair, Black's king has lost the right to castle, and you keep a clear advantage.
1652894211754070|h2h4.principle: 4...Bg6 handed you a real advantage, and an advantage has to be used at once: open lines against the uncastled king before Black untangles, instead of a slow wing plan.

1657768441002862|g7g6.headline: Knight first: 3...Nf6, then decide on the fianchetto
1657768441002862|g7g6.why: 3...g6 empties g7 before your knight or bishop can cover the long diagonal: after 4.d4 cxd4 5.Qxd4 the queen hits the rook on h8, and after 5...Nf6 6.Bb5+ Nc6 7.e5 dxe5 8.Qxd8+ you lose the right to castle. 3...Nf6, the most common master move (62.4%), develops and hits e4, so after 4.d4 cxd4 White recaptures with 5.Nxd4 and you reach a normal Open Sicilian, such as the Najdorf with 5...a6.
1657768441002862|g7g6.principle: The knight's best square, f6, is clear right away, while the bishop's depends on how the pawns settle; bring the knight out first and keep the fianchetto for later.

1783814385093536|d7d5.headline: Behind in development, keep it closed: 5...a6, not 5...d5
1783814385093536|d7d5.why: 5...d5 opens the centre while White has the lead in development: 6.Bb5+ Nc6 7.exd5 exd5 8.Ne5 Bd7 9.Qxd5 Nxe5 10.Qxe5+ wins back the gambit pawn with check to your king, and White is clearly better. Theory notes that after 4.Nxc3 White's development is simple while Black still needs pawn moves to catch up. 5...a6 is the useful one: it takes b5 away from White's bishop and knight, and after 6.Bf4 Nc6 7.Be2 d6 8.O-O Be7 you develop behind a compact pawn wall; masters choose it 42.2% of the time.
1783814385093536|d7d5.principle: When your opponent leads in development, keep the centre closed and finish developing before you open lines with a pawn break.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Nxc3

1783814385093536|f8b4.headline: Consolidate with 5...a6; 5...Bb4 gets hit by 6.Qd4
1783814385093536|f8b4.why: 5...Bb4 puts the bishop where nothing defends it: 6.Qd4 hits it and the g7 pawn at once, and after 6...Bf8 you have spent two moves to bring the bishop home, handing White the initiative. 5...a6, the most common master move (42.2%), keeps White's knight and bishop off b5, and you then develop calmly with ...Nc6, ...d6 and ...Be7, keeping the extra pawn in a level game. 5...Nc6, leading to the usual Smith-Morra main line, is just as good.
1783814385093536|f8b4.principle: You accepted the gambit, so consolidate: White leads in development and will hit any loose piece with tempo, so use modest, protected moves until your king is safe.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...e6/3. d4/3...cxd4

1890995340270663|d1d5.headline: Save the bishop with 9.Bb3, then develop by taking on c3
1890995340270663|d1d5.why: 8...Kf8 means Black can never castle, but the king now attacks your bishop on f7. 9.Qd5 holds it with the queen, but after 9...d6 10.Bxg8 Rxg8 11.Ng5 Qe8 12.Nxh7+ Ke7 the king walks out of danger and your edge shrinks. 9.Bb3 keeps the bishop on the same diagonal, and after 9...d6 10.Nxc3 you win the pawn back while developing a piece, keeping a large advantage. 9.Nxc3 is also good.
1890995340270663|d1d5.principle: With the enemy king already stuck in the centre, you don't need a queen raid; bring the rest of your pieces into play, ideally with moves that also win material.

1895778820316678|d1b3.headline: 8.Ba3 keeps Black's king from castling
1895778820316678|d1b3.why: 8.Qb3 brings the queen out with two minor pieces still at home, and Black simply castles with 8...O-O, taking the king away from f7; after 9.cxd4 Nxe4 Black has also taken your e4 pawn and is clearly better. 8.Ba3, the masters' choice 60% of the time, develops the bishop onto the open a3-f8 diagonal, where it covers f8 and stops Black from castling short. Black has to spend 8...d6 blocking it, and after 9.e5 Ne4 10.exd6 cxd6 11.Qe2 the e-file opens toward the king and the game stays close to level.
1895778820316678|d1b3.principle: When you have gambited for development, use it to keep the enemy king in the centre: a bishop that covers the castling squares is worth more than an early queen raid.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4/4...Bxb4/5. c3/5...Ba5/6. d4

1931050112551786|e6e5.headline: Just recapture with 4...exd5
1931050112551786|e6e5.why: 4...e5 leaves the d5 pawn alone and puts a second pawn where your opponent can take it: 5.fxe5 Qxd5 6.Nc3 leaves Black a pawn down with the queen already being chased, and White is close to winning. The d5 pawn is attacked twice and defended by nothing, so take it back with 4...exd5, keeping a pawn in the centre and a good game. After 5.Bb5+ Nc6 Black develops normally with ...Nf6 and ...Be7.
1931050112551786|e6e5.principle: When the opponent has just captured in the centre, look at the recapture first; a counter-push that ignores it usually loses material.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. f4

2067858163173673|d4c6.headline: Answer the threat on d4 with 6.Nb5, hitting c7
2067858163173673|d4c6.why: Black threatens 6...Qxd4, winning your knight, so it has to move. 6.Nxc6 dxc6 solves that, but it also helps Black: the c8 bishop is free, and after 7.O-O Be6 8.Bb3 Bc5 your edge is small. 5...Qf6 took the queen away from c7, so 6.Nb5 saves the knight with a threat of its own: a jump into c7 with check that would also hit the rook on a8. After 6...Bb4+ 7.Bd2 Bxd2+ 8.Nxd2 Kd8 Black guards c7 with the king and can no longer castle, and you keep a clear edge.
2067858163173673|d4c6.principle: When one of your pieces is attacked, look for the retreat that creates a threat of its own; it saves the piece and gains time instead of trading it for nothing.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...h6

2067858163173673|d4f3.headline: Save the d4 knight with a threat: 6.Nb5 hits c7
2067858163173673|d4f3.why: Black threatens 6...Qxd4, winning the knight, and 6.Nf3 saves it by moving it a second time with two minor pieces still at home; after 6...Bb4+ 7.Nbd2 Nge7 8.O-O O-O Black has caught up and the game is level. Theory notes that 3...h6 loses time, which 4.d4 exploits, so keep gaining time: 6.Nb5 saves the knight and attacks the pawn on c7. After 6...Bb4+ 7.Bd2 Bxd2+ 8.Nxd2 Black has to cover c7 with 8...Kd8, giving up castling, and you keep a clear advantage.
2067858163173673|d4f3.principle: If a piece has to move again, move it to a square where it wins something concrete or makes a threat, so the extra move costs your opponent time instead of you.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...h6

2094672111620588|d4e5.headline: Answer 3...f6 with 4.Bc4, aiming at the weakened light squares
2094672111620588|d4e5.why: 3...f6 holds e5 but costs a developing move and opens the a2-g8 diagonal toward Black's king. 4.dxe5 releases the tension: after 4...dxe5 the e5 pawn is firmly protected by the f6 pawn, and White's edge is small. 4.Bc4 develops onto that open diagonal, aiming through f7 at g8, where Black's king wants to castle; after 4...Nc6 5.h3 Nge7 6.O-O exd4 7.Nxd4 you have the extra development the theory says 3...f6 hands White, and a clear advantage.
2094672111620588|d4e5.principle: Black's ...f6 cost him development and weakened his king, so keep building your lead with developing moves and castling, and open the centre once your pieces are ready.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4

2107090482514507|c1e3.headline: Castle with 7.O-O to break the pin on c3
2107090482514507|c1e3.why: 6...Bb4 pins your knight on c3 to the king. 7.Be3 leaves the pin in place, and after 7...O-O 8.Qe2 Bxc3+ 9.bxc3 Black takes the knight with check and most of your edge is gone. 7.O-O breaks the pin by taking the king off the diagonal. Black can still swap on c3 later, as in 7...O-O 8.Qe2 b6 9.Bg5 Bxc3 10.bxc3, but by then your bishop on g5 pins the knight on f6 and you keep a clear edge; the theory notes that 3...Qd8 gives White a free hand to develop.
2107090482514507|c1e3.principle: Break a pin before the pinned piece is attacked again: castling takes your king off the b4-e1 diagonal and turns the knight on c3 back into a normal piece.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qd8

2122895618389281|c8f5.headline: Undermine the d5 pawn with 3...c6 before White consolidates
2122895618389281|c8f5.why: 3...Bf5 develops but leaves White's extra pawn alone: after 4.d4 e6 5.dxe6 fxe6 you are a pawn down with an isolated pawn on e6, and White is clearly better. Theory explains that White's 3.c4 is an attempt to hold the d5 pawn, and that Black's two main answers chip away at the pawn chain with 3...c6 or 3...e6. After 3...c6 4.d4 cxd5 you have the pawn back and the game has transposed into a Panov-Botvinnik Caro-Kann, which theory now rates as even; masters choose 3...c6 52.8% of the time.
2122895618389281|c8f5.principle: If you delay recapturing a gambit pawn, use your next move to win it back before your opponent can consolidate it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Nf6/3. c4

2162412998029713|f1c4.headline: 3...e6 prepares ...d5: put the bishop on d3, not c4
2162412998029713|f1c4.why: After 3...e6 Black is ready for ...d5, which hits a bishop on c4. In the line 4.Bc4 d5 5.exd5 exd5 6.Bd3 your bishop has to move again and Black has a free, equal centre, and most of your edge is gone. 4.Bd3 is the masters' top choice (28.9%): it develops the bishop toward the centre and defends e4 in advance, so after 4...Nc6 5.e5 White keeps space. 4.Nc3, 4.c3 and 4.Be2 also avoid the problem.
2162412998029713|f1c4.principle: Ask what your opponent's last move prepares; when ...e6 readies ...d5, develop your bishop to a square that the pawn push will not hit.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...g6/2. d4/2...Bg7

2179133986956493|f1c4.headline: e4 has no defender: develop with 5.Bd3, not 5.Bc4
2179133986956493|f1c4.why: Black threatens 5...Nxe4, and 5.Bc4 does nothing about it: the e4 pawn has no defender, so 5...Nxe4 wins it and Black is better. 5.Bd3, the masters' choice 84.3% of the time, develops the bishop toward the centre and guards e4 in the same move. After 5...O-O 6.O-O Nbd7 7.Re1 e5 8.h3 your centre of pawns on e4, d4 and c3 stands firm.
2179133986956493|f1c4.principle: Before picking a square for a developing piece, check what is loose: put the piece where it develops and also guards the undefended pawn.

2185447105552102|e1h1.headline: ...dxe4 forks d3 and f3: push 6.e5 before castling
2185447105552102|e1h1.why: 5...d5 threatens 6...dxe4, and that pawn would attack the bishop on d3 and the knight on f3 at once. 6.O-O ignores it: after 6...dxe4 7.Bxe4 Nxe4 you have lost a bishop, because once the d-pawn has gone the bishop on b7 also guards e4. 6.e5 (87.9% of masters games) takes the pawn out of the exchange, gains space by attacking the knight on f6 and leaves the b7 bishop blocked by Black's own pawn on d5; you keep a clear edge.
2185447105552102|e1h1.principle: Before a quiet move like castling, look at your opponent's captures; when a pawn capture would hit two of your pieces, resolve the central tension first.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...b6/2. d4/2...Bb7/3. Bd3/3...Nf6

221633201643279|d2d4.headline: 1...b5 hangs a pawn: take it with 2.Bxb5
221633201643279|d2d4.why: 2.d4 declines the free pawn, and after 2...Bb7 Black gets the queenside fianchetto at no cost, which gives back part of your advantage. The b5 pawn is attacked by your bishop and defended by nothing: 2.Bxb5 wins it and develops at the same time. The theory lists Black's ideas afterwards, ...Bb7 against your centre and ...a6 to kick the bishop (2...a6 3.Bc4), and they gain Black only a little time.
221633201643279|d2d4.principle: Take a gambit pawn when you can consolidate easily; here the capture is also a developing move, so there is nothing to consolidate.

2326611116094961|c1e3.headline: Answer the threat on d4 with 6.Bxf7+ check first
2326611116094961|c1e3.why: 5...Bc5 attacks your knight on d4 (6...Bxd4 is the threat), and 6.Be3 defends it but throws away a winning advantage and leaves the game roughly level. 6.Bxf7+ comes first: it takes the f7 pawn with check, and after 6...Kf8 Black can no longer castle. Then 7.Nxc6 moves the attacked knight with a capture that hits the queen, and you come out a pawn up against a stranded king.
2326611116094961|c1e3.principle: When the opponent makes a threat, check your own checks and captures before defending: a forcing move can solve the threat and gain material at the same time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...h6

2326611116094961|d4c6.headline: Check on f7 first: 6.Bxf7+ before trading knights
2326611116094961|d4c6.why: 3...h6 cost Black a tempo, and 5...Bc5 now attacks your knight on d4 twice, threatening 6...Bxd4. 6.Nxc6 answers the threat but lets the queen join with 6...Qf6, threatening mate on f2, and after 7.O-O dxc6 most of White's advantage is gone. 6.Bxf7+ first wins a pawn and drags the king to f8, where it can no longer castle; only then 7.Nxc6.
2326611116094961|d4c6.principle: Before answering a threat, check your own forcing moves: a check that wins something can come first.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...h6

2463215796795915|f1e2.headline: Take the undefended c5 pawn before Black trades it off: 6.dxc5
2463215796795915|f1e2.why: 6.Be2 lets Black release the tension with 6...cxd4 7.cxd4, which is what the theory says Black wants here, and your edge is gone. The c5 pawn is attacked once and defended by nothing, and the theory points out that 5...Bg4 does not stop you taking it: 6.dxc5. In the main line Black wins back the e5 pawn with 7...Nxe5, but 10.b4 then supports your pawn on c5 and gains space on the queenside, and you keep a small edge.
2463215796795915|f1e2.principle: Ask what your opponent wants: here Black wants ...cxd4 to free the position, so take on c5 first, which stops it and wins the undefended pawn.

2463215796795915|h2h3.headline: Don't spend a move on h3: take on c5 with 6.dxc5
2463215796795915|h2h3.why: 6.h3 invites 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3, and once the f3 knight is gone d4 has lost a defender: 7...cxd4 wins a pawn and Black is better. The pin on your knight does not need an answer yet; the theory points out that 5...Bg4 does not stop you taking on c5. The c5 pawn is attacked once and defended by nothing, so 6.dxc5 grabs it, and in the main line 10.b4 later supports it and gains queenside space.
2463215796795915|h2h3.principle: In the Advance, Black's play is aimed at the base of your chain, d4; don't help by inviting the exchange of its defender, and remove Black's c5 lever instead.

2465468553870240|c8f5.headline: Knight first: 5...Nc6, because ...Bf5 leaves b7 and d5 short
2465468553870240|c8f5.why: 5...Bf5 takes the bishop away from b7, and 6.Qb3 hits b7 and d5 at once: 6...Qb6 saves b7 but stops guarding d5, and 7.Nxd5 Nxd5 8.Qxd5 wins a pawn. 5...Nc6 is the main move (93% of master games): it develops toward the centre, adds pressure on d4, and keeps the bishop home until it can come out safely. The theory's line 5...Nc6 6.Bf4 Bf5 7.e3 e6 shows the bishop still reaches f5 a move later, and the game stays equal.
2465468553870240|c8f5.principle: In symmetrical positions the knight's square is obvious and the bishop's depends on the pawns, so develop the knight first and keep the bishop guarding b7 until its square is safe.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. cxd5/3...cxd5/4. Nc3/4...Nf6

2466581236058373|c8d7.headline: Block the check with 5...Nc6, keeping the queen guarding d5
2466581236058373|c8d7.why: After 5...Bd7, 6.Qe2+ forces 6...Qe7, and the queen on e7 no longer guards d5: 7.Bxd7+ Nxd7 8.Nxd5 Qxe2+ 9.Kxe2 leaves you a pawn down and White clearly better. 5...Nc6 (88% of masters games) blocks the check with the piece that wanted to go to c6 anyway, develops toward the centre and leaves the queen on d8 behind the d5 pawn. After 6.O-O Nf6 7.d4 Bd6 Black has a normal game, with only a small edge for White.
2466581236058373|c8d7.principle: Bring the knight to its natural square before committing a bishop; when you must block a check, block with the knight that was heading there anyway.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nc3/2...e6

2583228623150903|d7d5.headline: Knight on c3 and bishop on c4 hit d5: develop first
2583228623150903|d7d5.why: 2...e6 prepares ...d5, but with the knight on c3 and the bishop on c4 both aiming at d5, the push comes too early. After 3...d5 4.exd5 exd5 the d5 pawn has two attackers and only the queen defends it, so 5.Qe2+ Be7 6.Nxd5 wins it and White is clearly better. 3...Nc6 is the main move (48.3% of masters games): it develops toward the centre, and after 4.Nf3 Nf6 the game stays level.
2583228623150903|d7d5.principle: Before pushing a pawn to a contested square, count who attacks it and who defends it; here d5 is covered by the c3 knight and the c4 bishop, so it needs more support first.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nc3/2...e6

2615425569294719|c8f5.headline: ...Bf5 leaves b7 loose to Qb3: develop with 4...Nf6 first
2615425569294719|c8f5.why: 4...Bf5 takes the bishop off c8, where it was the only guard of b7, and 5.Qb3 attacks b7 and d5 together: after 5...Nc6 6.Nf3 Nf6 7.Qxb7 the b-pawn falls. 4...Nf6 is the main move (75.9% of master games): it develops toward the centre and adds a defender to d5. The bishop can still come to f5 later, as in 4...Nf6 5.Bf4 Nc6 6.Nf3 Bf5, once the knights are out.
2615425569294719|c8f5.principle: Before moving a piece, check what it stops guarding: the c8 bishop is b7's only defender, so it stays home until Qb3 no longer wins a pawn.

2671625836318681|b8c6.headline: Release the d5 tension with 5...dxe4 before it becomes a weak pawn
2671625836318681|b8c6.why: White threatens to win your d5 pawn with exd5, and 5...Nc6 doesn't stop it: after 6.exd5 exd5 7.Bb5 Bd7 8.Nxd5 the isolated d5 pawn falls and White is clearly better. With the d5 pawn under fire from the e4 pawn and the c3 knight, take first: 5...dxe4 claims the centre and leaves you with no weak pawn to defend. After 6.Nxe4 a6 7.Bd3 Be7 8.O-O Nf6 you develop smoothly and White's edge is small.
2671625836318681|b8c6.principle: When a centre pawn of yours is attacked and you cannot keep enough defenders on it, count the attackers and release the tension before it becomes an isolated target.

2692473875865858|c8f5.headline: In the Slav, 3...Nf6 first: an early ...Bf5 drops a pawn
2692473875865858|c8f5.why: Once the bishop leaves c8, b7 is undefended and a queen on b3 hits b7 and d5 together. Theory calls 3...Bf5 a grave mistake here: 4.cxd5 cxd5 5.Qb3 wins a pawn, and the engine's 4.Qb3 Qb6 5.Qxb6 axb6 6.cxd5 does the same. 3...Nf6, Black's most common reply by far, defends d5 and keeps the balance; the bishop can come out once ...e6 and the knight make it safe.
2692473875865858|c8f5.principle: Before developing a piece, check what it was guarding; in the Slav the c8 bishop holds b7, and Qb3 punishes it for leaving early.

269926073920586|c1e3.headline: Question the pinning bishop at once with 6.h3
269926073920586|c1e3.why: 6.Be3 lets Black keep the pin on your knight on f3 and finish developing with 6...e6 and 7...c6, and most of your advantage disappears. 6.h3, the choice in 89.9% of master games, asks the bishop on g4 to decide now: after 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3 you have the bishop pair and an active queen, then 8.Bd2 unpins the knight on c3 before 9.O-O-O, with a clear edge. If Black retreats instead, the theory shows the bishop being chased by g4 to g6.
269926073920586|c1e3.principle: A pin ties your knight to the queen; break it while it costs Black something, here by hitting the pinning bishop with the h-pawn before he can support it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qa5

269926073920586|f1e2.headline: Ask the g4 bishop at once with 6.h3
269926073920586|f1e2.why: 6.Be2 is not a blunder, but it lets Black finish ...Nbd7 and ...c6 before deciding about the bishop: after 6.Be2 Nbd7 7.a3 c6 8.h3 Bxf3 9.Bxf3 your edge shrinks to a small one. 6.h3 (89.9% of masters games) puts the question immediately. After 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3 you keep both bishops, your queen is already in play, and the plan 8.Bd2 and 9.O-O-O keeps a clear edge.
269926073920586|f1e2.principle: When an enemy bishop pins or eyes your knight from a square a pawn can attack, chase it with the pawn right away, while the trade still costs your opponent time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qa5

2731765578959899|c4b3.headline: 6.Bf1 guards g2 and hits b5: the refutation of 5...b5
2731765578959899|c4b3.why: 5...b5 deflects your bishop so Black can recapture on d5 with the queen, hitting g2. 6.Bb3 leaves g2 unguarded and lets the knight jump to d4 with tempo, 6...Nd4; after 7.d3 Bc5 Black is fully active and slightly better. 6.Bf1, played in 83.5% of master games, looks backward but guards g2 and attacks the b5 pawn: the theory shows that 6...Qxd5 then runs into 7.Nc3 with tempo, and after 6...Nxd5 7.Bxb5 you have picked up the pawn and keep a small edge.
2731765578959899|c4b3.principle: Ask what your opponent's move is for and stop it: Black's pawn offer aims at ...Qxd5 with an attack on g2, so put the bishop where it guards g2.

2731765578959899|c4b5.headline: Refute the Ulvestad with 6.Bf1: guard g2 and keep b5 in sight
2731765578959899|c4b5.why: 6.Bxb5 takes the bait: 6...Qxd5 attacks both your bishop and the g2 pawn, and after 7.Be2 Bb7 Black's pieces come out with tempo and the game is level. Theory explains that 5...b5 is offered to deflect your bishop from d5 and f7 so that Black can recapture with the queen. 6.Bf1 is the refutation: the bishop guards g2 and still eyes b5, your d5 pawn attacks the knight on c6, and if 6...Qxd5 then 7.Nc3 hits the queen with tempo. In the engine line 6...Nxd5 7.Bxb5 wins the pawn back anyway; masters choose 6.Bf1 83.5% of the time.
2731765578959899|c4b5.principle: Before grabbing a gambit pawn, check your opponent's forcing replies: a queen recapture that attacks two things at once is the whole point of the offer.

275585188789254|f3d4.headline: 5.e5 kicks the f6 knight before you collect d4
275585188789254|f3d4.why: 5.Nxd4 recaptures, but your e4 pawn has no defender and 5...Nxe4 takes it; after 6.Nxc6 bxc6 7.Qe2 Qe7 8.O-O Nd6 Black trades queens and is slightly better. Theory points out that Black is a pawn up here but has weaknesses: the e5 square, the knight on f6 and the f7 square. 5.e5, the masters' choice 70% of the time, uses them: it attacks the knight, and after 5...d5 6.Bb5 Ne4 7.Nxd4 you have won the pawn back with more space in the centre.
275585188789254|f3d4.principle: When your opponent's extra pawn comes with weaknesses, play on the weaknesses first; the pawn can usually be won back afterwards.

2781218480891122|g1f3.headline: Kick the e5 knight with 4.f4 and take the centre
2781218480891122|g1f3.why: After 3.d5 Ne5 the black knight sits in the centre with no pawn to support it. 4.Nf3 offers to trade it, and after 4...Nxf3+ 5.Qxf3 Black is relieved and White's big advantage shrinks. 4.f4 attacks it with a pawn instead: the knight retreats with 4...Ng6, and after 5.Nf3 d6 6.Nc3 you have a broad centre and a big space advantage.
2781218480891122|g1f3.principle: A knight in the centre without pawn support is a target: chase it with a pawn and gain space as it retreats.

2782228191759896|g1f3.headline: ...dxe4 is threatened: settle the centre with 5.e5 first
2782228191759896|g1f3.why: The pawn on d5 attacks e4, and nothing defends it, so 5.Nf3 simply loses it: 5...dxe4 6.Ne5 Bb4+ 7.Nc3 Ne7 and Black is a pawn up. 5.e5 (66.3% of masters games) takes the pawn out of the capture and claims space: backed by d4, it takes the f6 square from Black's knight, which has to go the long way with 6...Nge7 and 7...Nf5, and White keeps a small edge. 5.exd5 also keeps the material level.
2782228191759896|g1f3.principle: Before developing, check your opponent's captures: when a pawn attacks one of your central pawns, resolve the tension by advancing, exchanging or defending.

2790758909279175|d1e2.headline: ...g6 plus ...e6 leaves d6 weak: jump in with 8.Nb5
2790758909279175|d1e2.why: Theory flags 7...e6 as a mistake: combined with ...g6 it leaves the dark squares around Black's king, d6 above all, without a pawn to guard them. 8.Nb5 heads straight for d6: in the engine line 8...a6 9.Nd6+ Kf8 costs Black the right to castle, and theory's 8...Nf6 9.Qd6 threatens Nc7+. 8.Qe2 is a normal developing move but lets Black cover the hole with 8...a6 9.a4 Qc7, and most of White's advantage is gone.
2790758909279175|d1e2.principle: A square the opponent's pawns can no longer cover is an outpost; when ...e6 and ...g6 leave d6 unguarded, a knight landing there dominates.

2797760506254471|d2d3.headline: Refute the Latvian with 3.Nxe5: take the undefended pawn
2797760506254471|d2d3.why: 3.d3 defends e4 but lets Black keep the initiative in the centre: after 3...Nc6 4.d4 fxe4 5.Nxe5 Nf6 Black has the e4 pawn and easy development, and the game is level. Theory calls the Latvian utterly unsound: 2...f5 leaves the e5 pawn attacked once and not defended at all and opens the e8-h5 diagonal to Black's king. 3.Nxe5, played by masters 76.4% of the time, takes it, and Black dare not answer 3...fxe4 because of 4.Qh5+; after the main 3...Qf6 4.d4 d6 5.Nc4 fxe4 6.Nc3 Black has spent moves on the queen and pawns while you develop, and White is clearly better.
2797760506254471|d2d3.principle: Meet an unsound gambit by taking the material when your opponent's counterattack fails tactically, here because Black's king is exposed on the e8-h5 diagonal.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f5

2797760506254471|f1c4.headline: Refute the Latvian by taking e5 at once with 3.Nxe5
2797760506254471|f1c4.why: 3.Bc4 declines the gambit and lets Black carry out the idea behind 2...f5: after 3...fxe4 4.Nxe5 Qg5 the queen hits the knight on e5 and the pawn on g2 at once, and 5.d4 Qxg2 wins the pawn with a level game. 3.Nxe5 (76.4% of masters games) takes the undefended e-pawn right away. Black dare not reply 3...fxe4 because of 4.Qh5+, winning an exchange or more, so the main line is 3...Qf6 4.d4 d6 5.Nc4 fxe4 6.Nc3, and you keep a clear edge.
2797760506254471|f1c4.principle: Check captures first: when a gambit leaves a central pawn undefended and the capture also opens a check on the weakened e8-h5 diagonal, take it.

2861143771416580|e7e6.headline: 4.Bg5 leaves c4 hanging: take it with 4...dxc4
2861143771416580|e7e6.why: 4...e6 lets White keep a comfortable position: after 5.e3 h6 6.Bxf6 Qxf6 White's centre stands and White is slightly better. 4.Bg5 develops the bishop but leaves c4 attacked once and defended by nothing, so 4...dxc4, the most common master move (43.4%), wins a pawn. After 5.e3 b5 the pawn is backed by your queenside pawns, and 6...Qb6 and 7...a6 keep it supported, so Black is better.
2861143771416580|e7e6.principle: Accept a pawn when you can consolidate: here ...b5, ...a6 and ...Qb6 hold c4, and you finish developing afterwards.

2927847296126403|e7e6.headline: Take on f3 with 4...exf3 and keep the gambit pawn
2927847296126403|e7e6.why: White's f3 pawn attacks your e4 pawn, and 4.fxe4 would win back the gambit pawn. 4...e6 does nothing about it: after 5.fxe4 material is level, White has a broad pawn centre, and he is better. 4...exf3, the master choice in 78.7% of games, keeps the extra pawn; after 5.Nxf3 White has development for it, but you fianchetto with ...g6 and ...Bg7, castle, and stay a pawn up with the better game. 4...Bf5 and 4...e3 are also playable.
2927847296126403|e7e6.principle: Accept a gambit only if you can hold on to the pawn: here capturing on f3 keeps it, and a quick fianchetto and castling consolidate.

2973368771887475|f3e5.headline: Don't grab e5: 5.c3 kicks the knight and prepares d4
2973368771887475|f3e5.why: 5.Nxe5 takes the knight off the f-file, and 5...Qf6 at once threatens mate on f2 and hits the knight; after 6.O-O Qxe5 you have lost a knight for a pawn. Theory explains that the point of 4.b4 is to achieve c3 and d4 with tempo. 5.c3 does exactly that: it attacks the knight on b4, and after 5...Nc6 6.d4 exd4 7.cxd4 Bb6 you have the full pawn centre in return for the gambit pawn.
2973368771887475|f3e5.principle: Answer a capture of your gambit pawn with a pawn move that attacks the capturing piece and builds your centre, so you gain time while your opponent retreats.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4

3001047939008470|e7e5.headline: e5 has no defender here: play the solid 5...e6
3001047939008470|e7e5.why: 5...e5 puts a pawn where the d4 pawn and the f3 knight both attack it and nothing defends it: 6.dxe5 wins it and also kicks the knight on f6 back to d7. White then follows with 7.Nd4 against the bishop on f5 and 8.f4, and Black is close to lost. 5...e6 is the main move (58.1% of master games): your light-squared bishop is already outside the pawn chain on f5, so ...e6 supports d5 and opens the way for ...Be7, keeping the game level.
3001047939008470|e7e5.principle: Before a pawn break, count who attacks and who defends the square it lands on; a break that is attacked twice and defended zero times just loses the pawn.

3078274341826662|f3e5.headline: The d6 pawn guards e5: recapture on d4 instead
3078274341826662|f3e5.why: 6.Ne5 puts the knight where the pawn on d6 takes it: 6...dxe5, and 7.Qh5+ Kd7 8.Qxe5 does not win it back, leaving you a knight down. The Qh5+ trick that wins the rook on h8 in the 3...f5 line does not work here: Black answers 7.Qh5+ with 7...Kd7. Meanwhile d4 is attacked twice and not defended at all, so 6.Nxd4 (95.7% of masters games) wins the pawn back and centralises the knight, with a small edge for White.
3078274341826662|f3e5.principle: Moving a developed piece again is only worth it when it wins something concrete: here the knight's second move should collect the free pawn on d4, not walk into a pawn capture.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Bc4

3087437353600707|d1e2.headline: Open lines with 7.e5 before Black finishes developing
3087437353600707|d1e2.why: 6...Nf6 develops without first playing ...e6, which the theory says Black uses to blunt your bishop and prepare ...Be7 and castling. 7.Qe2 is too slow: 7...Bg4 pins your knight on f3 to the queen, Black swaps it with 9...Bxf3, and Black is slightly better. 7.e5, the top master choice (56.7%), hits the knight on f6; after 7...Ng4 8.exd6 exd6 Black's d6 pawn is isolated and the e-file opens for 11.Re1, which gives you full compensation for the pawn.
3087437353600707|d1e2.principle: You are a pawn down but ahead in development, so open lines while Black's king is still in the centre; a slow queen move gives him time to catch up.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Nxc3/4...Nc6/5. Nf3/5...d6/6. Bc4

3087437353600707|f3g5.headline: No Ng5 raid: 7.e5 hits the f6 knight instead
3087437353600707|f3g5.why: 7.Ng5 eyes f7, but one quiet move shuts the bishop on c4 out: after 7...e6 8.O-O Be7 9.Qe2 O-O 10.Nf3 the knight has gone back where it came from, two tempi wasted in a gambit, and Black is better. 7.e5 (56.7% of masters games) claims the centre and attacks the knight on f6. It also sets the trap from the theory notes: 7...Nxe5 8.Nxe5 dxe5 9.Bxf7+ Kxf7 10.Qxd8 wins Black's queen. After the main line 7...Ng4 8.exd6 exd6 9.O-O the game is balanced.
3087437353600707|f3g5.principle: Moving a developed piece again only pays when it wins something concrete; a knight sortie that one pawn move can parry just loses time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Nxc3/4...Nc6/5. Nf3

3179485995949204|c1f4.headline: Kick the f6 knight with 6.e5 once ...Be7 blocks its retreat
3179485995949204|c1f4.why: 6.Bf4 lets Black strike back with 6...c5, and after 7.Nc3 cxd4 8.Nxd4 your d4 pawn is traded off and much of your advantage goes with it. 5...Be7 was slow, and with the bishop on e7 the knight on f6 can no longer drop back to e7. 6.e5 gains space with tempo on the knight, which goes all the way back to g8 in the engine line, and after 7.O-O you are far ahead in development with a big advantage.
3179485995949204|c1f4.principle: A knight on f6 in front of an advanced e-pawn is a target: push the pawn when the knight has no good square, and you gain space and time together.

3179485995949204|e1h1.headline: Use your lead: 6.e5 sends the f6 knight back home
3179485995949204|e1h1.why: Black's 5...Be7 is passive and does nothing about the e4-e5 advance. 6.O-O is the most common move (83.3% of masters games), but it gives Black time for 6...O-O 7.c4 d5, and your large edge is cut in half. 6.e5 claims the centre and attacks the knight on f6; after 6...Ng8 the knight has to undo its development, and you keep a large advantage.
3179485995949204|e1h1.principle: When your opponent's quiet move hands you a clear advantage, act on it at once with a forcing advance; a routine move gives them the time to catch up.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...b6/2. d4/2...Bb7/3. Bd3

3350501418691275|a7a6.headline: Cover e5 with 5...d6 so your f6 knight can't be kicked
3350501418691275|a7a6.why: 5...a6 does nothing about e5, so 6.e5 drives your knight all the way back to g8, and after 7.Bf4 Ne7 8.Bd3 Ng6 9.Bg3 White has a big lead in development and is clearly better. Theory stresses finding out how White deals with the e4 pawn before moving more pawns, and once White has played Nc3 the push e5 is the danger. 5...d6, the masters' choice 54.9% of the time, takes e5 under control, so the knight stays on f6 and keeps pressing e4; after 6.g4 h6 7.Rg1 Nc6 8.Be3 Bd7 you later strike back with 9...d5.
3350501418691275|a7a6.principle: Before a useful-looking pawn move, ask what your opponent wants next; here it is e5 to kick your knight, so control that square first.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...e6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4/4...Nf6

3400735200665154|g5f7.headline: Take on f7 with the bishop, with check: 5.Bxf7+
3400735200665154|g5f7.why: 4...Nxe4 grabs a pawn but leaves f7 defended only by the king. 5.Nxf7 looks tempting because it forks the queen and rook, but 5...Qh4 threatens mate on f2, and after 6.Qe2 Nd4 7.g3 Nxe2 8.gxh4 Nd4 9.Nxh8 Black's knight forks on c2 and your edge is gone. 5.Bxf7+ takes with check instead: after 5...Ke7 Black can no longer castle, and 6.d4 means Black can't yet take on g5 without losing the queen.
3400735200665154|g5f7.principle: f7 is defended only by the king at the start; when your opponent neglects it, take there with the piece that gives check and keep your attackers.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...Nxe4

3415269394174453|b2b4.headline: No Evans here: 5.d3 develops, 5.b4 just drops a pawn
3415269394174453|b2b4.why: 5.b4 offers an Evans-style pawn, but the follow-up of hitting the bishop with c3 is impossible with your knight already on c3: 5...Bxb4 simply wins a pawn, and after 6.Nd5 O-O 7.Nxb4 Nxb4 Black stays a pawn up and is better. 5.d3, the masters' choice 88.4% of the time, guards e4 and opens the diagonal for your c1 bishop. After 5...a6 6.O-O d6 7.a4 you have a solid position with the game level.
3415269394174453|b2b4.principle: In the opening, play the pawn moves that free your pieces and support the centre; a flank pawn push that neither develops nor gains time just costs material.

3420590449456095|c1e3.headline: Pin the c6 knight with 6.Bb5 before ...e5 arrives
3420590449456095|c1e3.why: 5...Nc6 adds pressure on d4 and prepares ...e5, which the theory says the queen on a5 supports. 6.Be3 lets Black carry it out: after 6...Bg4 7.h3 Bxf3 8.Qxf3 O-O-O 9.O-O-O e5 10.d5 Nd4 his knight lands in the centre and Black has active play. 6.Bb5, the most popular master move (48%), pins the knight on c6 to the king so it cannot join the fight for d4, and if Black lets you take it, 8.Bxc6+ bxc6 leaves him with doubled c-pawns.
3420590449456095|c1e3.principle: A pin ties down two pieces at once: pin the knight that is doing Black's work against d4, and his central break loses its support.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qa5

3420590449456095|f1d3.headline: Black is eyeing d4: pin the c6 knight with 6.Bb5
3420590449456095|f1d3.why: Your d4 pawn is defended by the queen and the knight on f3, and 6.Bd3 cuts the queen off. Black goes straight for the other defender: 6...Bg4 7.Bd2 O-O-O 8.Nb5 Qb6 9.a4 Bxf3 10.Qxf3 Nxd4, and Black has won the pawn and is slightly better. 6.Bb5, the masters' top choice (48%), develops the bishop and pins the knight on c6 to the king, so it cannot join an attack on d4. 6.Bd2 is also good.
3420590449456095|f1d3.principle: Ask what your opponent is preparing: here ...Nc6, ...Bg4 and ...O-O-O all aim at d4, so develop with a move that takes one of those attackers out of the game.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qa5

3451177064254537|d8b6.headline: Strike with 6...d5 instead of an early queen move
3451177064254537|d8b6.why: White threatens to push d5 and win a pawn, and 6...Qb6 brings the queen out with three minor pieces still at home instead; after 7.O-O Nf6 8.Nc3 Be7 9.d5 exd5 10.exd5 Ne5 11.Nxe5 the centre opens with your king still uncastled and White is clearly better. 6...d5 claims the centre and attacks both the bishop on c4 and the pawn on e4, so White has to react. After 7.exd5 exd5 8.Bb3 Bb4+ 9.Nc3 Nf6 10.O-O you develop with tempo and the game is level.
3451177064254537|d8b6.principle: Don't spend a move on the queen while your minor pieces are at home; a central pawn break that attacks something does more and keeps the queen safe.

3451177064254537|g8f6.headline: Hit White's two-pawn centre at once with 6...d5
3451177064254537|g8f6.why: After 6.cxd4 White has pawns on e4 and d4, and the push d4-d5 against your knight on c6 is a real threat. 6...Nf6 lets the centre roll: 7.Qe2 Be7 8.e5 Nd5 drives your knight away and White gains space and a comfortable edge. 6...d5 claims the centre and attacks both the bishop on c4 and the pawn on e4; after 7.exd5 exd5 8.Bb3 Bb4+ 9.Nc3 Nf6 your pieces come out freely and the game is level.
3451177064254537|g8f6.principle: When your opponent builds a two-pawn centre, strike at it with a pawn before it advances and gains space with tempo.

3472532178632675|f1b5.headline: Put the bishop on c4: 5...e5 left f7 weak
3472532178632675|f1b5.why: 5...e5 does nothing for f7, unlike the main move ...e6, which the theory says relieves the bishop's pressure there. 6.Bb5 aims at the knight on c6 instead: after 6...Be7 7.Qa4 Nf6 8.O-O d6 Black simply develops, and even when 9.Bxc6+ bxc6 10.Qxc6+ Bd7 wins the pawn back, Black has the bishop pair and the better game. 6.Bc4 puts the bishop on its best diagonal, the move the theory's plan for White calls for; if 6...Nf6, then 7.Ng5 d5 8.exd5 wins the pawn back with a strong initiative, and White is clearly better.
3472532178632675|f1b5.principle: Develop each piece to the square where it does the most: in the Morra the bishop belongs on c4, especially once ...e5 has left f7 without help.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Nxc3/4...Nc6/5. Nf3

3516647903289485|f8d6.headline: Knight to f6 first: 6...Bd6 gets hit by e4 and d4
3516647903289485|f8d6.why: After 6...Bd6 7.e4 the pawn hits your bishop and d5 together, and 8.d4 opens the centre while your pieces are still loose; after 9.exd5 cxd5 10.Nb5 Bb8 11.dxe5 your centre has broken up and White is clearly better. 6...Ngf6 develops the knight toward the centre and adds a guard against e4. After 7.e4 dxe4 8.Nxe4 Nxe4 9.dxe4 Be6 pieces come off and the game stays level.
3516647903289485|f8d6.principle: Bring out the knight whose square is obvious before committing a bishop that can become a target for the opponent's central pawns.

3540159667319526|b7b6.headline: Develop with 5...Nc6 instead of spending a tempo on ...b6
3540159667319526|b7b6.why: 5...b6 is a pawn move that neither develops nor holds anything, and White uses the time: 6.dxc5 Bxc5 7.b4 drives the bishop back, and after 7...Be7 8.Bb5+ Kf8 your king has lost the right to castle, and White is clearly better. 5...Nc6 is the main move (70.2% of masters games): it develops a piece and adds pressure on d4. 5...Nf6 and 5...Bd6 are fine developing alternatives.
3540159667319526|b7b6.principle: In an open position, only move the pawns that free your pieces or fight for the centre; a flank pawn move costs a tempo your opponent can turn into threats against your king.

3586492073419954|g7g6.headline: Develop 6...Be7; ...g6 after ...e6 weakens your dark squares
3586492073419954|g7g6.why: With ...e6 and ...d6 already played, 6...g6 leaves the dark squares around your king with no pawn cover: 7.Bg5 at once pins the knight on f6 to your queen, and after 7...Nbd7 8.Qe2 h6 9.Be3 e5 you have spent several pawn moves and White is clearly better. 6...Be7, the main master move (55.3%), develops, covers the dark squares and breaks any pin in advance, so you can castle next; after 7.Be3 a6 8.Bb3 b5 9.f3 O-O you have a normal Sicilian and a roughly level game.
3586492073419954|g7g6.principle: Only make the pawn moves you need: once ...e6 is played, ...g6 leaves holes on the dark squares, so develop the bishop to e7 and castle instead.

362391570447215|c5d4.headline: 4.d4 drops e4: take it with 4...dxe4
362391570447215|c5d4.why: 4...cxd4 releases the tension in White's favour: after 5.exd5 exd5 6.Bb5+ Nc6 7.Nxd4 you are left with an isolated pawn on d5, White develops with checks like 8.Qe2+, and the edge passes to White. 4.d4 abandoned the e4 pawn, which is attacked once and not defended at all. 4...dxe4 wins it and kicks the knight, and after 5.Ne5 Nf6 6.Bb5+ Bd7 7.Nxd7 Nbxd7 you have developed smoothly and kept the extra pawn.
362391570447215|c5d4.principle: Every time your opponent changes the pawn structure, check what is newly undefended; a loose centre pawn is worth taking before anything else.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...e6

3692429315258999|c4e2.headline: Challenge the pinning bishop with 6.h3 instead of retreating
3692429315258999|c4e2.why: Black threatens 6...dxe5 to win the pawn back, and 6.Be2 doesn't stop it; it also moves the bishop a second time with two minor pieces still at home, and after 6...dxe5 the game is level. 5...Bg4 pins your f3 knight to the queen, so ask the bishop at once: 6.h3 attacks it, and in the engine line Black gives it up with 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3. After 7...Nxe5 8.Qe2 Nxc4 9.Qxc4 c6 10.Nc3 your queen is active, Black's light-squared bishop is gone and you keep the lead in development.
3692429315258999|c4e2.principle: When a bishop pins your knight to the queen, question it with h3 before it does damage, rather than spending a move on a passive interposition.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...d6

3699514865674152|d1e2.headline: 7.Ng5 hits f7 twice and wins the gambit pawn back
3699514865674152|d1e2.why: The theory explains that Black usually plays ...e6 to relieve your bishop's pressure on f7; ...e5 and ...Nf6 leave f7 guarded only by the king. 7.Qe2 is too slow: Black plays 7...Be7 and castles, f7 is safe, and with the gambit pawn in hand he is slightly better. 7.Ng5 hits f7 a second time, so Black answers 7...d5 to block the bishop, but 8.Bxd5 Nxd5 9.exd5 wins the pawn back and your d5 pawn hits the knight on c6, leaving White clearly better.
3699514865674152|d1e2.principle: Moving the knight a second time is justified when it wins something concrete: here it doubles the attack on f7 and forces Black to give the pawn back.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Nxc3/4...Nc6/5. Nf3

3699514865674152|e1h1.headline: ...e5 leaves f7 exposed: 7.Ng5 before castling
3699514865674152|e1h1.why: 7.O-O is natural but slow: Black gets 7...Be7 and castles, your gambit compensation is gone and Black keeps the extra pawn. Black chose ...e5 rather than ...e6, which the theory notes would have relieved the bishop's pressure on f7, so 7.Ng5 hits f7 a second time while only the king defends it. In the main line Black blocks with 7...d5, and 8.Bxd5 Nxd5 9.exd5 wins a pawn back with the better game.
3699514865674152|e1h1.principle: When the opponent leaves the bishop on c4 staring at f7, add a second attacker before you castle; f7 is defended only by the king.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Nxc3/4...Nc6/5. Nf3

3726374757153429|f1c4.headline: 5.Bg5 pins the e7 knight and stops 5...Nec6
3726374757153429|f1c4.why: 5.Bc4 lets Black untangle at once with 5...Nec6, and after 6.Nc3 Be7 7.Nd5 Nxd4 8.Qxd4 O-O the knights are traded and Black is comfortable, so half your edge is gone. 4...Ne7 blocks the f8 bishop, and 5.Bg5 pins that knight to the queen on d8, so it cannot move without losing the queen. Black spends 5...h6 chasing the bishop, and after 6.Be3 Nec6 7.Nc3 Be7 8.Nd5 O-O 9.Nb5 your knights take over d5 and b5 while Black's knight ends up on a6.
3726374757153429|f1c4.principle: Develop your bishop to a square where it pins or attacks, so the opponent has to spend a move answering it instead of carrying out his plan.

3800718395256466|c6d5.headline: Recapture 7...Nxd5 and keep c6 guarding b5
3800718395256466|c6d5.why: 7...cxd5 removes the pawn that kept White's knight out of b5: 8.Nb5 threatens a fork on c7, Black has to answer 8...Kd8, and after 9.Ne5 Bg6 10.Nxa7 White's rook on a1 helps win the a7 pawn, leaving White clearly better. 7...Nxd5 takes back the pawn, which was attacked twice and defended only by the knight on c3, and leaves the c6 pawn in place. After 8.e4 Nxc3 9.exf5 Nd5 material is level and White's edge is small.
3800718395256466|c6d5.principle: In a queenless position judge the differences: 7.axb3 gave White a half-open a-file against a7, so keep the c6 pawn covering b5 and recapture with a piece.

3815488023003540|b8c6.headline: Resolve the tension with 5...cxd4 before d5 kicks your knight
3815488023003540|b8c6.why: 5...Nc6 leaves the c5 and d4 pawns facing each other, and White pushes past with 6.d5: the knight is hit and goes to the rim with 6...Na5, and the pawn on d5 cramps Black, giving White a clear advantage. 5...cxd4 trades your flank pawn for White's centre pawn and claims the centre. After 6.a4 b4 7.Nxd4 Black has the half-open c-file and develops comfortably with 7...Qc7 and 8...Nf6, with a level game.
3815488023003540|b8c6.principle: Before putting a knight in front of the opponent's centre pawns, check whether a pawn advance can hit it; trading that pawn off first removes the threat.

3903276797068408|a2a3.headline: Take on c5 now: 7.dxc5 wins a pawn
3903276797068408|a2a3.why: 7.a3 is too slow: after 7...Bxf3 8.Qxf3 Qb6 Black's queen hits b2 and backs up the attack on d4, and the position tips slightly in Black's favour. The theory notes explain that White threatens to take on c5 and that ...Bg4 does not stop it, so Black should have released the tension with ...cxd4. 7.dxc5 takes the pawn while it is there, and after 7...Bxf3 8.Qxf3 you are a pawn up with a small edge.
3903276797068408|a2a3.principle: In the Advance structure Black aims every break at the base of your chain on d4; when the pawn attacking it can be captured for free, take it instead of letting the pressure build.

3903276797068408|h2h3.headline: Take on c5 with 7.dxc5 before Black liquidates
3903276797068408|h2h3.why: 7.h3 invites 7...Bxf3, and after 8.gxf3 Qb6 your kingside pawns are doubled, Black's queen hits b2 and Black is better. Theory notes that in this line White keeps threatening to take on c5, which is why Black should liquidate the tension with ...cxd4. 6...e6 didn't, so take now: 7.dxc5 wins a pawn, and after 7...Bxf3 8.Qxf3 you recapture with the queen and keep your pawn structure intact.
3903276797068408|h2h3.principle: Look at captures before quiet moves: when your opponent leaves the central tension in place, the capture may simply win a pawn.

397857285398425|d5d4.headline: Keep the tension with 4...Nc6; 4...d4 hands White e4
397857285398425|d5d4.why: 4...d4 kicks the knight, but your pawn no longer covers e4, so the knight jumps straight there with 5.Ne4, and after 5...Nc6 6.d3 f5 7.exf6 Nxf6 8.g3 the game is level. 4.e5 has given you a French-type structure, and 4...Nc6, the main master move (77.3%), develops and aims at d4; in the line 5.Nf3 Bd7 6.d4 Nh6 7.Ne2 Qb6 8.c3 f6 Black piles up on d4, then hits e5 with ...f6, and is slightly better.
397857285398425|d5d4.principle: Against a pawn chain, keep your own pawns where they are and aim your pieces at its base: here the knight on c6 and queen on b6 work against d4.

4040334401902569|c4e2.headline: Hit the pinning bishop with 5.h3, then kick the knight with d5
4040334401902569|c4e2.why: 4...Bg4 threatens to remove the defender of d4: after 5.Be2 Bxf3 6.Bxf3 Nxd4 you are a pawn down and your bishop has moved twice for nothing. 5.h3 questions the bishop at once. After 5...Bh5, 6.d5 takes the pawn out of the attack with tempo on the knight, which goes back to 6...Nb8, and you keep a big space advantage and develop easily with 7.Be3.
4040334401902569|c4e2.principle: When the opponent's pieces sit where your pawns can hit them, push with tempo: h3 and d5 gain space while the bishop and knight lose time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...d6

4040334401902569|d4e5.headline: Break the pin with 5.h3 instead of releasing the centre
4040334401902569|d4e5.why: In the Paris Defence White has the extra space, and 4...Bg4 pins your f3 knight to the queen, so d4 is only defended in name and Black threatens 5...Nxd4. 5.dxe5 solves that by trading your space away: after 5...dxe5 most of White's advantage is gone. 5.h3 questions the bishop at once, and after 5...Bh5 6.d5 you gain even more space with tempo on the knight.
4040334401902569|d4e5.principle: When a bishop pins your knight to the queen, everything that knight guards is loose; break the pin, usually with h3, before your opponent cashes in.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...d6

4141510809291242|d7d5.headline: 1.c4 targets d5: develop with 1...Nf6 instead
4141510809291242|d7d5.why: 1.c4 discourages 1...d5, and the theory notes say that capturing the pawn gives White a small advantage: after 2.cxd5 Nf6 3.d4 c6 4.dxc6 Nxc6 White has traded the c-pawn for your centre pawn and is a pawn up. 1...Nf6 is the most popular reply (27.7% of masters games): it develops toward the centre, controls d5 and e4 with a piece, and keeps your options open; after 2.d4 the game can turn into an Indian defence. 1...e5, 1...e6 and 1...c5 are also good.
4141510809291242|d7d5.principle: Your king's knight's best square is clear from move one, while the right pawn setup depends on what White does next; so develop the knight first and choose the pawn moves later.
