4149982820903367|e8h8.headline: Release the tension with 7...dxc4 before White strips d5's defenders
4149982820903367|e8h8.why: White threatens to win a pawn on d5, and 7...O-O doesn't stop it: after 8.Bxf6 Bxf6 9.Bxf5 exf5 10.cxd5 White's two bishop trades remove the knight and pawn that guarded d5, and you are a pawn down. 7...dxc4 takes the target away first and makes the d3 bishop move a second time with 8.Bxc4. Then 8...h6 9.Bh4 Ne4 forces trades that free your position, and after 10.Nxe4 Bxe4 11.Bxe7 Qxe7 the game is level.
4149982820903367|e8h8.principle: Count the defenders of a centre pawn under pressure, including pieces your opponent can exchange off, and release the tension before a routine move like castling.

4164085910631465|c1g5.headline: Rebuild the Evans centre: take back with 8.cxd4
4164085910631465|c1g5.why: You are two pawns down here, and the Evans Gambit pays for them with the centre. 8.Bg5 leaves the d4 pawn alone, and after 8...dxc3 9.Nxc3 you are still two pawns down with only the e4 pawn left in the middle, and Black is better. The pawn on d4 is attacked three times and defended twice, so 8.cxd4 wins one pawn back and puts pawns on e4 and d4, the centre 6.d4 was aiming for; White keeps a small edge.
4164085910631465|c1g5.principle: In a gambit, the material you gave is paid for by the centre and development; whenever a pawn capture lets you rebuild the centre, take it before developing further.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4/4...Bxb4/5. c3/5...Bc5

4164085910631465|c4f7.headline: Win d4 back with 8.cxd4 instead of sacrificing on f7
4164085910631465|c4f7.why: 8.Bxf7+ Kxf7 9.cxd4 gives a bishop for two pawns, and Black is better. 7...Nge7 left the d4 pawn attacked three times and defended only twice, so you can simply take it back: 8.cxd4 rebuilds the e4-d4 centre the gambit was played for and hits the bishop on c5, which retreats with 8...Bb6. Then 9.Ng5 adds a second attacker to f7 while Black's king is still on e8, and you keep the advantage.
4164085910631465|c4f7.principle: The Evans Gambit gives a pawn for a big centre and fast development, so when you can win the centre pawn back cleanly, do that before any sacrifice.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4/4...Bxb4/5. c3/5...Bc5

4175344914430296|e7e5.headline: Nothing defends e5: play the solid 4...e6
4175344914430296|e7e5.why: 4...e5 puts a pawn where the knight on f3 attacks it and nothing of yours defends it, so 5.Nxe5 simply wins it, and after 5...Bd6 6.Nf3 Nf6 White is clearly better. 4...e6, the masters' top choice (43.2%), backs up d5, opens the way for the f8 bishop and keeps the game level. 4...Nf6 and 4...h6 are also fine.
4175344914430296|e7e5.principle: Before pushing a pawn into the centre, count who attacks the square and who defends it; a pawn on e5 facing a knight with no defender is just lost.

4211428648959227|c5d4.headline: Recapture 4...exd5 at once; 4...cxd4 leaves White's d5 pawn alive
4211428648959227|c5d4.why: The white pawn on d5 is attacked twice and defended by nothing, so take it back now. 4...cxd4 lets it live: after 5.Bb5+ Bd7 6.dxe6 fxe6 7.cxd4 your e6 pawn is isolated, the c3 square is free for White's knight again, and White is clearly better. 4...exd5, played in 89.8% of master games, recaptures and opens a diagonal for your c8 bishop, and the game stays level; the theory notes that Black is in no hurry to play ...cxd4, because that frees c3 for White's knight.
4211428648959227|c5d4.principle: Recapture toward the centre: taking on d5 with the e-pawn restores your central pawn and frees a bishop, while ...cxd4 hands White's pieces the c3 square.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. c3

4237788959769826|c1e3.headline: Kick the f6 knight with 10.e5, then develop with 11.Bf4
4237788959769826|c1e3.why: 10.Be3 puts the bishop where 10...Ng4 attacks it, and after 11.Rac1 Nxe3 12.Qxe3 Black has the bishop pair and the better game. 10.e5 claims the centre and attacks the knight on f6, which retreats to e8 in the engine line. Then 11.Bf4 develops the last minor piece behind the e5 pawn, and after 11...a6 12.Bb3 b5 13.Rac1 your pieces are all in play while Black's are pushed back.
4237788959769826|c1e3.principle: A knight on f6 in front of your e-pawn is a target: the push gains space and drives it back, and your bishop can then develop behind the pawn.

4245409631012417|d4e5.headline: Bg5 first: hit the queen before opening the d-file
4245409631012417|d4e5.why: 5.dxe5 opens the d-file too early: after 5...dxe5 6.Bg5 Qd6 7.Nxe5 Qxd1+ 8.Rxd1 the queens come off, and with them goes Black's main problem, the misplaced queen. You still have a large advantage, but a smaller one. 5.Bg5 first develops the bishop with an attack on the queen on f6; after 5...Qg6 6.dxe5 you win a pawn with the queens still on, and 7.Qd2 and 9.O-O-O follow, keeping a large advantage.
4245409631012417|d4e5.principle: Develop with threats while the opponent's queen is exposed; release the central tension only after it has gained you time, not in a way that lets the queen trade itself off.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Qf6

4245409631012417|f1c4.headline: Hit the early queen: 5.Bg5 develops with tempo
4245409631012417|f1c4.why: 5.Bc4 lets Black pin your knight with 5...Bg4, and after 6.Bg5 Bxf3 7.Qd2 Qg6 8.gxf3 exd4 your kingside pawns are split and Black has taken the d4 pawn; your large advantage is cut in half. The theory notes on 2...Qf6 say an early queen gives the opponent chances to develop with tempo. 5.Bg5 does exactly that: it develops the bishop and attacks the queen on f6, and after 5...Qg6 6.dxe5 you win a pawn and keep a large advantage.
4245409631012417|f1c4.principle: When your opponent brings the queen out early, look for developing moves that attack it; each one gains a tempo and often wins material.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Qf6

425955225904234|g7g6.headline: Answer 5.f3 with 5...e5, kicking the d4 knight
425955225904234|g7g6.why: 5...g6 ignores what 5.f3 is for: White keeps the option of c4 and gets an easy set-up with 6.Nc3 Nc6 7.Be3, and after 7...h5 8.h3 h4 9.Bc4 White is better. Theory gives 5...e5 as the main reply: it claims the centre and attacks the knight on d4, so White spends 6.Nb3, and Black can then contest c4 with ...Be6 and ...Rc8 or prepare ...d5. After 6...Be7 7.c4 a5 8.Be3 O-O you are developed and the game is level; masters play 5...e5 57.5% of the time.
425955225904234|g7g6.principle: A knight in the centre that a pawn can attack is a target: the push gains space and time, and here it also stops White from playing e5.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4/4...Nf6

4292473947156740|e4d5.headline: Defend e4 with 4.Nbd2; 4.exd5 frees Black's bishop
4292473947156740|e4d5.why: Black threatens 4...dxe4. 4.exd5 answers it by swapping, but after 4...exd5 the position is symmetrical, Black's c8 bishop has an open diagonal, and your edge almost disappears. 4.Nbd2 defends e4 with a developing move and keeps the tension; after 4...Nf6 5.Bd3 c5 6.e5 Nfd7 7.c3 you have a French structure with extra space and d4 well supported. 4.e5 is also fine.
4292473947156740|e4d5.principle: When a centre pawn is attacked, defend it with a developing piece rather than exchanging it, because the exchange only frees your opponent's pieces.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. d4

4293527898658762|g1f3.headline: Recapture 4.cxd4: keep the e4-d4 centre instead of gambiting
4293527898658762|g1f3.why: The pawn on d4 is attacked twice, by your c3 pawn and queen, and nothing defends it. 4.Nf3 leaves it there and Black answers 4...dxc3, so after 5.Nxc3 you are playing a Smith-Morra a pawn down, with your edge gone. 4.cxd4, played in 97.3% of master games, takes back and gives you two centre pawns side by side; after 4...d5 5.e5 you reach a French-style structure with more space and a small edge.
4293527898658762|g1f3.principle: When your opponent trades a wing pawn for a centre pawn, recapture toward the centre so your pawns on e4 and d4 stand together.

4304063535539389|g7g6.headline: Take d5 away from the c3 knight: 7...e6
4304063535539389|g7g6.why: 7...g6 leaves d5 uncovered, and 8.Nd5 lands there at once: after 8...Nd7 White builds up freely with 9.Qd2, 10.f3 and 12.h4 and has a clear edge. 7...e6 is the main move (63.7% of master games): the e-pawn takes d5 away from the knight on c3 and opens e7 for the bishop (9...Be7), so Black can castle quickly with 11...O-O. 7...e5, hitting the knight on d4, is also fine.
4304063535539389|g7g6.principle: Ask where your opponent's pieces want to go before you set up your own plan: here White's knight wants d5, so take that square away first.

4424038725631884|g1f3.headline: Break the pin on e2 with tempo: 5.d4 hits the queen
4424038725631884|g1f3.why: The bishop on e2 is pinned by the queen on e5, so after 5.Nf3 Bxf3 you can only take back with 6.gxf3, your kingside pawns are broken and the advantage passes to Black. 5.d4 attacks the pinning queen with a central pawn: after 5...Bxe2 6.Ngxe2 you recapture with a developing move, the queen still has to move, and 7.b4 gains more time on it. The theory says ...Qe5+ achieves little for exactly this reason: the queen blocks Black's e-pawn and gets chased again.
4424038725631884|g1f3.principle: An early queen in the centre is a target: attack it with pawns and pieces that also develop or free your position, and each time it must move you gain a tempo.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3

4444685778052974|e7e5.headline: 6...e5 hands White the d5 square: play 6...e6
4444685778052974|e7e5.why: 6...e5 kicks the knight, but it goes forward to 7.Nf5, and after 7...Nc6 8.Qf3 Bxf5 9.exf5 Be7 10.Bxf6 Bxf6 11.Bd3 you have given up your light-squared bishop. With your pawns on d6 and e5 and no c-pawn, d5 can never be attacked by a black pawn again, and White is clearly better. 6...e6 (78.2% of masters games) is the main answer to 6.Bg5: it frees the queen and the f8 bishop to cover f6, so your pawns cannot be doubled, and the e6 pawn keeps watch over d5 and f5. 6...Nbd7 is also playable.
4444685778052974|e7e5.principle: Before pushing a pawn, check which squares it can no longer guard; ...e5 here turns d5 into a permanent outpost for White's pieces.

4444685778052974|h7h6.headline: Against 6.Bg5, prepare to recapture on f6: play 6...e6
4444685778052974|h7h6.why: 6...h6 does nothing about the threat to your pawn structure: 7.Bxf6 gxf6 doubles your f-pawns and opens the kingside, and 8.Qh5 aims straight at it, giving White a clear edge. The theory says Black must react to 6.Bg5 to avoid doubled f-pawns, and 6...e6 is the almost universal answer (78.2% of master games). It opens the queen's line to f6, so a capture there can be met by the queen, and it prepares ...Be7; 6...Nbd7 solves the same problem with the knight.
4444685778052974|h7h6.principle: Spend your pawn moves on pawns that free your pieces: ...e6 opens lines for the queen and bishop, while ...h6 only asks a question that White is happy to answer.

4491386101925356|c5c4.headline: Capture toward the centre: 3...cxd4 is the point of the Sicilian
4491386101925356|c5c4.why: 3...c4 leaves the pawn with no support, and 4.Bxc4 simply takes it while developing, so you are a pawn down for nothing and White is clearly better. 3...cxd4, played in 99.8% of master games, captures toward the centre with a flank pawn and breaks up White's two-pawn centre. After 4.Nxd4 you have two central pawns to White's one and the half-open c-file, and 4...Nc6 5.Nc3 Qc7 leads into a normal Taimanov.
4491386101925356|c5c4.principle: Trade a flank pawn for an enemy centre pawn whenever you can: it leaves you more pawns in the middle and opens a file for your rooks.

4491386101925356|d7d5.headline: Trade your c-pawn for White's centre pawn: 3...cxd4
4491386101925356|d7d5.why: 3...d5 opens the position before you have developed: after 4.exd5 exd5 5.Bb5+ Nc6 6.O-O Nf6 7.Nc3 Bg4 8.Bg5 all of White's pieces are out, both of your knights are pinned, and White is clearly better. 3...cxd4 (99.8% of masters games) captures toward the centre with a flank pawn and breaks up White's two-pawn centre. After 4.Nxd4 you have two central pawns to White's one and the half-open c-file, and you can choose your ...e6 Sicilian.
4491386101925356|d7d5.principle: Trade a wing pawn for a centre pawn whenever you can: it breaks up your opponent's centre and leaves you with more central pawns for the middlegame.

4513314094589663|b1c3.headline: 8.Bxf7+ and queen checks pick up the loose c5 bishop
4513314094589663|b1c3.why: 8.Nxc3 is natural, but after 8...d6 the bishop on c5 is defended and most of your advantage is gone. 7...dxc3 spent another move on a pawn while that bishop stood undefended next to an uncastled king. 8.Bxf7+ Kxf7 9.Qd5+ checks the king and hits the bishop, and after 9...Ke8 10.Qh5+ Kf8 11.Qxc5+ you have the piece back, the f7 pawn is gone and Black can no longer castle; 12.Qxc3 then collects the c3 pawn too.
4513314094589663|b1c3.principle: Look at checks first, especially when an enemy piece is undefended: a check that also attacks the loose piece wins it back with interest.

4552034363865958|d7d5.headline: Behind in development, keep the centre closed: play 4...a6
4552034363865958|d7d5.why: White already has a knight in the centre and is ready to develop the bishops, while you have nothing out. 4...d5 opens lines for White: 5.Bb5+ Bd7 6.exd5 exd5 7.O-O Bc5 8.Re1+ Ne7 9.Nf5 leaves your king stuck on the open e-file, and White is clearly better. 4...a6, the Kan, is the masters' top choice (39.8%): it takes b5 away from White's pieces, so that Bb5+ is gone, and Black develops only after White commits. 4...Nc6 and 4...Nf6 are the other main moves.
4552034363865958|d7d5.principle: When you are behind in development, keep the position closed until your pieces are out; opening the centre helps the side that is already developed.

4559296915298785|f1d3.headline: Bd3 cuts the queen off from d4: develop with 6.Nf3
4559296915298785|f1d3.why: Your d4 pawn is defended only by the queen on d1, and 6.Bd3 blocks that line. 6...Qxd4 takes it, and 7.Bxf5 Qe5+ 8.Be4 Nxe4 leaves you a pawn down, because the queen check also hits the bishop. 6.Nf3 develops toward the centre and defends d4; it also punishes 5...Bf5, which left b7 without its defender, since after 6...e6 7.Qb3 your queen attacks it, with a clear edge.
4559296915298785|f1d3.principle: Develop the king's knight before the bishop: Nf3 has an obvious square that guards d4, while a bishop on d3 can block your own queen's defence.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Nf6/3. d4

4572718139339834|c1a3.headline: Castle first: the e7 queen eyes e4 with check
4572718139339834|c1a3.why: The queen on e7 attacks e4, which nothing defends, and your king is on the same file. 8.Ba3 attacks the queen, but she answers 8...Qxe4+, taking the pawn with check, and after 9.Kd1 you have also lost the right to castle, and Black is much better. 8.O-O (100% of masters games) takes the king off the e-file first; in the main line the bishop still reaches a3 later, with 12.Ba3, once the king is safe; the game is balanced.
4572718139339834|c1a3.principle: Get your king off the open e-file before starting play elsewhere; a central king turns every enemy capture on that file into a check.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4/4...Bxb4/5. c3/5...Ba5/6. d4

4572718139339834|c1g5.headline: Castle with 8.O-O before attacking; 8.Bg5 allows 8...Qxe4+
4572718139339834|c1g5.why: 8.Bg5 hits the queen, but she steps aside with 8...Qxe4+, taking a pawn with check because your king still stands on the e-file; after 9.Kf1 you have lost the right to castle and Black is clearly better. 8.O-O, the only move masters play here, takes the king off the e-file first, and your lead in development pays for the gambit pawn: after 9.cxd4 Nxd4 10.Nxd4 Bxd4 you bring out the rest with 11.Nc3 and 12.Ba3, with balanced chances.
4572718139339834|c1g5.principle: In a gambit the e-file opens quickly, so castle before you start attacking; while the king sits on e1, every loose centre pawn can be taken with check.

4572718139339834|f3g5.headline: Castle with 8.O-O; a lone knight raid on f7 just loses e4
4572718139339834|f3g5.why: 8.Ng5 moves the knight a second time and achieves nothing: 8...Nh6 covers f7, the knight has to go back with 10.Nf3, and 10...Qxe4 takes your centre pawn, leaving you two pawns down without compensation. In the Evans you have given a pawn for time, so spend it on 8.O-O, the move every master game in the database chose. After 8...Bb6 9.cxd4 you rebuild the centre, and 11.Nc3 and 12.Ba3 bring out your last minor pieces with full compensation.
4572718139339834|f3g5.principle: In a gambit the centre opens fast and Black's queen already stands on the e-file, so castle before starting an attack with a single piece.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4/4...Bxb4/5. c3/5...Ba5/6. d4

4603395450140279|g1f3.headline: 3...Nc6 declines the gambit: recapture with 4.cxd4
4603395450140279|g1f3.why: The Smith-Morra offers a pawn for development, but 3...Nc6 hasn't taken it. 4.cxd4 recaptures and gives you the classical pawn centre on d4 and e4, which masters choose 96% of the time. 4.Nf3 lets Black take after all with 4...dxc3 5.Nxc3, reaching the regular Smith-Morra a pawn down when you could have had the centre for free.
4603395450140279|g1f3.principle: When your opponent declines a gambit pawn, take it back and build the centre; there is no reason to offer it again.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3

4670522513947528|h2h4.headline: 4...e6 lets you take on f5: play 5.Bxf5
4670522513947528|h2h4.why: 5.h4 lets Black trade bishops on their own terms: after 5...Bxd3 6.Qxd3 c5 Black strikes at the base of your chain, and the game is level. The theory notes call 4...e6 a highly unusual reply, and with ...e6 already played, the only way to recapture after 5.Bxf5 is 5...exf5. That leaves Black with doubled f-pawns for the rest of the game, and you keep a clear edge.
4670522513947528|h2h4.principle: Judge trades by the structure they leave: when a capture forces your opponent to recapture with a pawn and double it, that lasting difference favours you.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. e5/3...Bf5/4. Bd3/4...e6

4675628834516483|f1d3.headline: Don't block the queen's guard of d4: 5.Be2, not 5.Bd3
4675628834516483|f1d3.why: Black's c5 pawn and knight on c6 both attack d4, and 5.Bd3 cuts the queen off from defending it: after 5...cxd4 6.cxd4 Nxd4 the pawn is simply gone, and with it your opening edge. 5.Be2, the most popular master move (45.9%), keeps the d-file open and, as the theory says, waits for Black's light-squared bishop to commit before 6.Nf3. With the bishop on e2, a later ...Bg4 no longer pins the knight on f3 to your queen.
4675628834516483|f1d3.principle: In the Advance structure Black piles up on d4, so before every move count its attackers and defenders, and never cut one of your defenders off.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. e5/3...c5/4. c3/4...Nc6

4781739738408769|b1c3.headline: Look for checks: 9.Qd5+ forks the king and the e5 knight
4781739738408769|b1c3.why: 8...Nxe5 leaves the knight on e5 undefended while the black king stands exposed on f7. 9.Nbc3 develops but lets Black tidy up with 9...Kg8, and most of your advantage is gone. 9.Qd5+ gives check and attacks the knight at the same time: the king has to go to g6, and 10.Qxe5 wins a whole piece.
4781739738408769|b1c3.principle: Check every check before you develop: a queen check that also hits a loose piece is a fork, and an exposed king makes those checks easy to find.

4845873281403230|d7d5.headline: Develop with 3...Nc6 before opening the centre with ...d5
4845873281403230|d7d5.why: 3...d5 opens the centre while your kingside pieces are still at home: after 4.exd5 exd5 5.Bb5+ Nc6 White pins the knight, and 8.Bxc6+ comes later to damage your pawns. 3.b3 is slow and does nothing about d4, so 3...Nc6 develops toward the centre first. If 4.Bb5, then 4...Nge7 lets you recapture on c6 with a knight, as in 6.Bxc6 Nxc6, and after 7.d4 cxd4 8.Nxd4 you have a comfortable Sicilian.
4845873281403230|d7d5.principle: Your king is still on e8 with no kingside piece out, so keep the centre closed and develop the knights before a break like ...d5 lets White check on b5.

4870221886044145|e1h1.headline: 5...e6 made e4 a target: guard it with 6.Bd3 before castling
4870221886044145|e1h1.why: 5...e6 blunts your bishop on c4, and e4 is attacked by the bishop on b7 with nothing defending it, so 6.O-O allows 6...Bxe4, a clean pawn. 6.Bd3 moves the blunted bishop to a square where it guards e4, and you keep a comfortable centre: after 6...d6 7.O-O Ne7 8.Re1 the rook adds a second defender. 6.Qe2 also holds the pawn.
4870221886044145|e1h1.principle: After every opponent move, quiet ones included, ask what it now threatens; here ...e6 shut out your bishop, so e4 needs a defender before you castle.

4879166842565878|c1g5.headline: d4 is attacked three times, defended twice: take it with 8.cxd4
4879166842565878|c1g5.why: 8.Bg5 develops with an attack on the queen but does nothing about d4: 8...f6 blocks and hits the bishop, and after 9.cxd4 Nxd4 10.Nxd4 fxg5 the exchanges favour Black, who keeps the extra pawns. d4 is attacked three times and defended only twice, so 8.cxd4 wins the pawn back at once and gives you the e4 and d4 pawn centre. In the main line 8...Bb6 9.h3 Na5 10.Bd3 keeps your bishop, and 11.Nc3 completes your development with a balanced game.
4879166842565878|c1g5.principle: Count attackers and defenders on the central pawn first: when a capture wins it back outright, take it before making developing moves elsewhere.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4/4...Bxb4/5. c3/5...Bc5

4879166842565878|f1e1.headline: Two pawns down in the Evans: recapture 8.cxd4 now
4879166842565878|f1e1.why: You have given two pawns for the centre, and 8.Re1 does nothing to get one back: Black pins your knight with 8...Bg4, and after 9.e5 d5 10.Be2 dxc3 11.Nxc3 you are still two pawns down with no centre to show for it, and Black is clearly better. The pawn on d4 is attacked three times and defended twice, so 8.cxd4 wins it and gives you pawns on e4 and d4, the centre the Evans Gambit is played for.
4879166842565878|f1e1.principle: Count attackers and defenders on the pawn in the middle of the board: three against two means you can take it, and here taking it also rebuilds your centre.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4/4...Bxb4/5. c3/5...Bc5

4879166842565878|f3g5.headline: Rebuild the centre with 8.cxd4; d4 is attacked three times
4879166842565878|f3g5.why: 8.Ng5 moves the knight a second time with two minor pieces still at home, and 8...Nh6 covers f7 at once; then 9...dxc3 takes another pawn and Black castles in peace, clearly better. d4 is attacked three times and defended only twice, so 8.cxd4 wins the pawn back and gives you pawns on d4 and e4, the centre that is your compensation in the Evans. In the main line the bishop retreats with 8...Bb6, and you keep developing with 10.Bd3 and 11.Nc3.
4879166842565878|f3g5.principle: In a gambit your compensation is the centre: when you can recapture toward it with a pawn, do so before starting an attack with single pieces.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4/4...Bxb4/5. c3/5...Bc5

4886445385944472|c2c3.headline: Resolve the tension with 3.dxe5; 3.c3 invites ...d5
4886445385944472|c2c3.why: Black threatens 3...Nxd4, and 3.c3 holds the pawn but lets Black hit back with 3...d5; after 4.dxe5 Be6 5.exd5 Qxd5 6.Nf3 Qxd1+ 7.Kxd1 O-O-O+ the queens are off, your king is in the open and your advantage has vanished. Theory says that both pushing the pawn and taking on e5 are very good for White. 3.dxe5, played by masters 43% of the time, liquidates the centre on your terms: the knight recaptures with 3...Nxe5, and after 4.Nc3 Bc5 5.f4 your pawn kicks it again with gain of space.
4886445385944472|c2c3.principle: When your opponent attacks a centre pawn twice, settle the tension on your terms by exchanging or advancing, rather than propping the pawn up in a way that lets him open the centre himself.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nc6/2. d4/2...e5

4907156095699170|c8f5.headline: Nothing guards f5: 3...Bf5 just hangs the bishop
4907156095699170|c8f5.why: 3...Bf5 puts the bishop on a square the bishop on d3 attacks, and no black piece or pawn defends f5, so 4.Bxf5 wins a whole bishop. Offering the bishop trade only works when you can recapture. 3...Nf6 develops toward the centre and controls e4; the light-squared bishop still gets out later, as in 3...Nf6 4.Nf3 Bg4, and the game is level.
4907156095699170|c8f5.principle: Before putting a piece on a new square, check whether an enemy piece attacks it there and whether you can recapture; an undefended piece facing an attacker is simply lost.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5

4920065110243890|c2c3.headline: 2...e5 hangs a pawn: take it with 3.dxe5
4920065110243890|c2c3.why: 3.c3 offers a gambit against a move that already hangs a pawn: after 3...exd4 Black wins the d-pawn anyway, and a winning position turns into a level one. The theory says Black should play 2...cxd4; 2...e5 instead leaves the e5 pawn attacked once and defended by nothing. 3.dxe5 takes it and claims the centre, and since your pawn has left d4, the threat of 3...cxd4 disappears with it.
4920065110243890|c2c3.principle: When both sides have pawns en prise, look at the captures first: taking with your attacked pawn wins material and removes the opponent's threat in one move.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4

4920065110243890|d4d5.headline: 2...e5 leaves e5 hanging: take it with 3.dxe5
4920065110243890|d4d5.why: Black's 2...e5 is a mistake: the theory notes say Black should take with 2...cxd4, and here the pawn on e5 is attacked by your d4 pawn and defended by nothing. 3.d5 does answer Black's threat of 3...cxd4, but it passes up the free pawn and closes the centre; after 3...Nf6 4.Nd2 Be7 your large edge is cut by more than half. 3.dxe5 removes the threat and wins the pawn at the same time, keeping a large advantage.
4920065110243890|d4d5.principle: After every opponent move, check what it left undefended; a capture that wins a loose pawn and removes a threat beats a move that only parries the threat.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4

4981514382355858|b8c6.headline: Accept with 3...dxc3 or decline properly; 3...Nc6 does neither
4981514382355858|b8c6.why: 3...Nc6 does not stop 4.cxd4, so White gets the pawn back for free and has the ideal pawns on e4 and d4; after 4...d5 5.exd5 Qxd5 6.Nf3 e5 7.Nc3 White develops with gain of time and is better. 3...dxc3 accepts the gambit (54.5% of masters games and the engines' choice): after 4.Nxc3 you are a pawn up, and White's lead in development is the price, with the game level. If you prefer to decline, 3...Nf6 heads for an Alapin Sicilian.
4981514382355858|b8c6.principle: Facing a gambit, decide: take the pawn if you can consolidate, or decline with a move that stops your opponent's ideal centre; a neutral move gives them the centre without any sacrifice.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3

5083117640380754|b8c6.headline: Answer c3 by hitting e4 at once: 3...Nf6
5083117640380754|b8c6.why: 3...Nc6 puts no pressure on e4, so White plays 4.d4 straight away and after 4...cxd4 5.cxd4 has the two-pawn centre that 3.c3 was preparing, with a clear edge. 3...Nf6 attacks e4 first, and with a pawn on c3 White can no longer bring a knight to c3 to defend it. White has to deal with e4 before anything else, and in the main line d4 only arrives with 8.d4, with the game level.
5083117640380754|b8c6.principle: When White plays c3 to prepare d4, contest the centre immediately with a developing move that attacks e4, so the pawn centre never gets built for free.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. c3

5083117640380754|e7e6.headline: Hit e4 with 3...Nf6 before White's d4 arrives
5083117640380754|e7e6.why: 3.c3 prepares d4 for a full pawn centre and blunts the long diagonal a later ...Bg7 would use. 3...e6 lets White build it: after 4.d4 Nc6 5.d5 White gains space, your knight retreats with 6...Nce7, and White is comfortably better. 3...Nf6 attacks e4 at once, so White must look after it before pushing d4; masters play it 98.6% of the time and the position stays level.
5083117640380754|e7e6.principle: Develop with a threat against the centre: a knight attacking e4 makes White spend time defending instead of building the d4 centre.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. c3

5092403403866739|b8c6.headline: Take on d4 first: 4...cxd4, or White takes on c5
5092403403866739|b8c6.why: 4...Nc6 allows 5.dxc5, which wins a pawn: recapturing with the d-pawn opens the d-file for a queen trade with check, as in the game line 8...dxc5 9.Qxd8+, and White has a large advantage. 4...cxd4 is played in 99.9% of master games: it trades your c-pawn for White's centre pawn, which is the point of 1...c5. After 5.Nxd4 a6 6.Be3 Nf6 Black develops normally.
5092403403866739|b8c6.principle: When pawns attack each other in the centre, look at the captures first: if you don't take on d4, White takes on c5.

513248652268614|c1e3.headline: 10.Nb5 hits the queen and d6, winning the pawn back
513248652268614|c1e3.why: 9...Qc7 puts the queen where your knight can hit it from b5, and the d6 pawn already faces your rook on d1. 10.Be3 is a natural developing move but lets Black castle with 10...O-O, and Black is slightly better. 10.Nb5 attacks the queen on c7 and adds a second attacker to d6; after 10...Qb8 11.Bf4 e5 12.Bg5 O-O 13.Bxf6 Bxf6 14.Nxd6 you win the gambit pawn back and keep a small edge.
513248652268614|c1e3.principle: Count the attackers on d6: your rook on d1 already hits it, so adding the knight while chasing away the queen, one of its defenders, tips the count your way.

5136765216062701|f1c4.headline: Put the bishop on d3, or go 5.h4, not 5.Bc4
5136765216062701|f1c4.why: With Black's pawn on e6, ...d5 is coming, and 5.Bc4 puts your bishop where that pawn hits it: after 5...d5 6.exd5 exd5 7.Bd3 you have spent two moves to reach d3. 5.Bd3 goes there directly, and the engine's 5.h4 uses the idea theory credits to Fischer against the Modern: push the h-pawn to loosen the fianchetto before Black castles.
5136765216062701|f1c4.principle: Develop a piece straight to the square where it will end up; if a pawn push will chase it, you'll have to move it twice.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...g6/2. d4/2...Bg7

5143411063260921|d8b6.headline: Guard d5 with 7...e6; 7...Qb6 drops it to 8.Nxd5
5143411063260921|d8b6.why: White's queen on b3 eyes b7, and the knight on c3 eyes d5. 7...Qb6 covers b7 but takes your queen off the d-file, so 8.Nxd5 wins the d5 pawn with tempo on the queen and White is clearly better. 7...e6 gives d5 a solid pawn defender and frees your f8 bishop; if White plays 8.e4 Bxe4 9.Qxb7, you have taken the e4 pawn in return and keep developing with 9...Nd7 and 10...Rc8, with a level game.
5143411063260921|d8b6.principle: With two minor pieces still at home, a queen sortie becomes a target; defend the centre with a pawn and develop instead.

5165721780484766|d2d3.headline: Against the French, build the two-pawn centre with 2.d4
5165721780484766|d2d3.why: 2.d3 is a sideline that lets Black take an equal share of the centre: after 2...d5 3.Nf3 dxe4 4.dxe4 Qxd1+ 5.Kxd1 the queens are gone, your king has lost the right to castle, and the game is level. The theory says White almost always answers 1...e6 with 2.d4 (89.5% of master games): it puts a second pawn in the centre and opens lines for both bishops and the queen. After 2...d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e5 you gain space, and 5.f4 supports the e5 pawn.
5165721780484766|d2d3.principle: When the opponent lets you, occupy the centre with two pawns; a timid pawn move hands Black the central share 1...e6 was preparing for.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6

5169185492904926|c8f5.headline: The c8 bishop guards b7: play 3...Nf6 first
5169185492904926|c8f5.why: 3...Bf5 takes away the only defender of b7, and 4.Qb3 attacks it at once. 4...Qc7 holds, but after 5.cxd5 cxd5 6.Nc3 White's queen, knight and the bishop on g2 all aim at d5, Black has to cover it with 6...e6, and White is better. 3...Nf6 (87.1% of masters games) develops toward the centre and adds a defender to d5, and after 4.Nf3 g6 5.b3 Bg7 your kingside is ready to castle.
5169185492904926|c8f5.principle: Before moving a piece, check what it was defending; when White's queen can reach b3, the c8 bishop is b7's only guard.

5184811817876652|e1h1.headline: 6.O-O drops e4: chase the knight with 6.e5 first
5184811817876652|e1h1.why: Black threatens 6...Nxe4, and 6.O-O doesn't stop it: the knight on f6 and the bishop on b7 both hit e4, so after 6.O-O Nxe4 you are a pawn down and Black is better. 5...Nf6 made that threat, but it also put the knight in front of your e-pawn. 6.e5 claims the centre and attacks the knight, which in the engine line ends up on the rim after 6...Ng4 7.Na3 Qc8 8.h3 Nh6; you gain space and keep a clear advantage.
5184811817876652|e1h1.principle: Check your opponent's captures before a quiet move like castling, and look for an answer that meets the threat with a threat of your own.

5215145015608227|c8f5.headline: Develop the knight first; 4...Bf5 lets Qb3 hit b7 and d5
5215145015608227|c8f5.why: 4...Bf5 takes away b7's only defender while d5 is already eyed by the bishop on g2: 5.Qb3 hits both, and in the game line Black ties the queen to b7 with 5...Qc8 and answers 6.Nc3 with 6...e6, a passive setup that gives White the edge. 4...Nc6 develops toward the centre and keeps the bishop guarding b7 a little longer. After 5.d4 the bishop comes out with 5...Bf5 anyway, followed by ...Nf6 and ...e6, with a good game.
5215145015608227|c8f5.principle: In these symmetrical structures bring the knights out before the light-squared bishop: the bishop is guarding b7, and its best square can wait until the queenside is safe.

5231539809808326|e6e5.headline: Recapture 4...Qxd5; 4...e5 just hangs a pawn to the knight
5231539809808326|e6e5.why: 4...e5 puts a pawn on a square the knight on f3 attacks and nothing defends: 5.Nxe5 wins it, and after 5...Qxd5 6.Bb5+ Bd7 7.Nxd7 you are a pawn down and clearly worse. 4...Qxd5, the most common master move (58.5%), takes back the pawn on d5, which your queen and e6 pawn both attack. With White's pawn on c3, his knight cannot hit your queen from c3, and in the main line it goes to a3 instead, as in 5.Na3 Nf6 6.d4 Nc6. Recapturing with 4...exd5, as the theory describes for 2...e6, is also good.
5231539809808326|e6e5.principle: Count attackers and defenders before moving a centre pawn: d5 is attacked twice and defended by nothing, while e5 would be attacked by the knight and defended by nothing.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...e6

5254169560142503|c1d2.headline: Use your gambit lead: 7.Ng5 hits f7 instead of passive 7.Bd2
5254169560142503|c1d2.why: 7.Bd2 answers the pin on c3 passively: Black develops with 7...Nf6 and castles, your gambit compensation runs out and Black is simply a pawn up. In the Smith-Morra you are a pawn down for a lead in development, so use it: 7.Ng5 joins the bishop on c4 against f7, which only the king defends, and in the main line Black has to spend 7...Nh6 guarding it. After 8.O-O O-O 9.Qh5 a third piece aims at f7 and the position stays in your favour.
5254169560142503|c1d2.principle: A gambit's compensation is time, and it disappears if you play passively; use the lead to attack the weak point f7 before Black castles.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Nxc3

5265791031076490|b5d7.headline: 7.Qe2 guards the b5 bishop and hits e5 at once
5265791031076490|b5d7.why: 6...Bd7 threatens 7...Bxb5, winning a bishop, but 7.Bxd7+ answers it by trading your only developed bishop and bringing Black's queen out with 7...Qxd7; after 8.O-O O-O-O 9.d4 Nxd5 Black is quickly developed and stands better. The point of 5...Na5 was to chase your bishop, so keep it and make Black react instead. 7.Qe2 covers b5 along the diagonal and attacks the pawn on e5, so Black spends 7...Bd6 defending it; only then do you trade with 8.Bxd7+ Qxd7 9.Nc3, and the game stays balanced.
5265791031076490|b5d7.principle: When a piece is attacked, look first for a defending move that also creates a threat, so your opponent has to answer you instead of developing.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...d5/5. exd5/5...Na5

5269510306588935|f1c4.headline: Kick the knight with 6.e5 before ...Nc6 covers e5
5269510306588935|f1c4.why: 5...Nf6 puts the knight where your e-pawn can hit it. 6.Bc4 is natural but lets Black cover e5 first with 6...Nc6, so after 7.e5 the knight has 7...Ng4 and the game is level. 6.e5 kicks it at once: in the engine line it goes all the way back with 6...Ng8, and after 7.Bc4 d5 8.exd6 Bxd6 9.O-O you have a big lead in development for the pawn. The theory gives the same idea against an early ...Nf6 in the Morra: e5 is a free tempo that embarrasses Black.
5269510306588935|f1c4.principle: A knight that a pawn can attack is a target: push the pawn while the knight has no good square, before Black adds a defender to the push square.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Nxc3

5286148894410756|d3c2.headline: Release the tension with 7.dxc5; don't move the bishop twice
5286148894410756|d3c2.why: Black's c5 pawn, knight on c6 and queen on b6 all hit d4, and your bishop on d3 blocks the queen's defence, so 7...cxd4 is a real threat. 7.Bc2 moves the bishop again without solving it: after 7...cxd4 8.cxd4 Nb4 the knight swaps off that bishop with 9...Nxc2, and Black is slightly better. 7.dxc5, the top master choice (51.3%), removes the target: after 7...Bxc5 8.O-O you are castled, the e5 pawn still cramps Black, and 10.Nbd2 and 11.Nb3 bring the knight to hit the bishop on c5, keeping a small edge.
5286148894410756|d3c2.principle: With the knight on b1 and bishop on c1 still at home, a second move with the same bishop must win something; here it only gives Black time to cash in on d4.

5414391277109696|b1c3.headline: Bishop on g4 is loose: 5.Bxf7+ and 6.Ng5+ win it back
5414391277109696|b1c3.why: 4...Bg4 leaves the bishop undefended on the diagonal of your queen, with only the knight on f3 in between. 5.Bxf7+ Kxf7 6.Ng5+ moves that knight with check, so after 6...Ke8 7.Qxg4 you have your piece back, Black can no longer castle, and after 7...Bxd4 8.Qe6 your queen and knight on g5 stand next to the stuck king, with a large advantage. 5.Nc3 is normal development but misses it, and after 5...e6 6.Be3 Nc6 7.Qd2 Bxf3 your edge shrinks to a small one.
5414391277109696|b1c3.principle: Early on the king alone guards f7; when a bishop sacrifice there is followed by a knight check that uncovers your queen on a loose piece, play it.

5414391277109696|c2c3.headline: 5.Bxf7+ and 6.Ng5+ win back the loose g4 bishop
5414391277109696|c2c3.why: 4...Bg4 left the bishop undefended and f7 guarded only by the king. 5.c3 is too quiet: Black covers f7 with 5...e6, later swaps with 7...Bxf3, and most of your advantage is gone. 5.Bxf7+ Kxf7 6.Ng5+ moves the knight off the queen's diagonal with check, so 7.Qxg4 wins the piece back; after 7...Bxd4 8.Qe6 Black's king is stuck in the centre with your queen and knight next to it, and White is close to winning.
5414391277109696|c2c3.principle: f7 is defended only by the king, so with a bishop on c4 and a knight ready for g5, always check a sacrifice there, especially when a loose piece can be collected afterwards.

5414391277109696|h2h3.headline: Don't ask with 5.h3: 5.Bxf7+ exploits the undefended g4 bishop
5414391277109696|h2h3.why: 5.h3 lets Black solve his problems by swapping: after 5...Bxf3 6.Qxf3 e6 f7 is covered and your big chance has passed. The bishop on g4 has no defender, so strike at once with 5.Bxf7+ Kxf7 6.Ng5+: the knight leaves with check, your queen's diagonal to g4 opens, and 7.Qxg4 takes the bishop back. After 7...Bxd4 8.Qe6 Black can no longer castle, his king faces your queen and knight, and White is close to winning.
5414391277109696|h2h3.principle: When an enemy piece is undefended, look for a check that unblocks one of your pieces against it; here the sacrifice on f7 and the knight check do exactly that.

5530528877961804|f3d4.headline: Meet 3...e4 with 4.Qe2: pin the pawn, don't retreat
5530528877961804|f3d4.why: 3...e4 kicks your knight and threatens 4...exf3, hoping to seize the initiative. 4.Nd4 saves the knight but moves it a second time and gives back the d5 pawn to 4...Qxd5, and White's advantage is gone. 4.Qe2, the masters' choice in 75.4% of games, attacks the e4 pawn and pins it to the king on e8, so it can't take your knight, and 5.d3 then undermines Black's advanced pawn.
5530528877961804|f3d4.principle: When a pawn attacks your piece, look for a pin on that pawn before retreating; a pinned pawn can't capture.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d5/3. exd5/3...e4

5580466240815728|c8f5.headline: Same Slav rule: knight to f6 before the bishop leaves c8
5580466240815728|c8f5.why: Theory is blunt here too: avoid 3...Bf5, because 4.cxd5 cxd5 5.Qb3 attacks b7 and d5 at once and wins a pawn; after 5...Nf6 6.Qxb7 White later takes on a7 as well. 3...Nf6 is by far the most common reply: the knight controls e4 and adds a defender to d5, keeping the position level.
5580466240815728|c8f5.principle: Knights before bishops: in the Slav the knight on f6 defends d5 and covers e4, while the c8 bishop's best moment comes later.

5588080788603958|c7c6.headline: 2...dxe4 takes a pawn White cannot win straight back
5588080788603958|c7c6.why: 2...c6 declines the gambit into a Caro-Kann, and after 3.e5 Bf5 White gets an Advance-style position with extra space, so the small edge you had passes to White. After 2.e4 the e4 pawn is attacked once and not defended at all, and theory rates the Blackmar-Diemer as suspect at professional level: there is no way for White to win the pawn back immediately. After 2...dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 you develop with the extra pawn, and if White tries 3.f3 instead, 3...e5 is the strong answer.
5588080788603958|c7c6.principle: Accept a gambit when you can develop normally afterwards; here ...Nf6 and ...Bf5 come naturally, so the pawn is a clean gain.

5641703819423939|c8f5.headline: 4.f3 leaves c4 undefended: take it with 4...dxc4
5641703819423939|c8f5.why: After 4.f3 the c4 pawn is attacked by your d5 pawn and has no defender. 4...Bf5 walks into 5.g4: after 5...Bc8 6.g5 Nh5 7.e4 White has chased your pieces back and built a big centre with gain of time, and stands better. 4...dxc4 takes the pawn now, and your c6 pawn supports 7...b5 to hold it, so you stay a pawn up with the better game.
5641703819423939|c8f5.principle: Once f3 is played, White's g-pawn can chase a bishop on f5 with tempo, so do not develop it into that pawn storm; grab the loose c4 pawn instead.

57158813525553|f1d3.headline: The c5 pawn is loose: take it with 5.dxc5
57158813525553|f1d3.why: 4...Bf5 develops but leaves the pawn on c5 attacked by your d4 pawn and defended by nothing. 5.Bd3 lets the chance pass: after 5...Bxd3 6.Qxd3 e6 7.Nf3 Nd7 Black has time to cover c5, so when White does take with 9.dxc5 Black recaptures with 9...Nxc5 and the game is level. The theory notes say Black should first add pressure with 4...Nc6; without it, 5.dxc5 wins a clean pawn, and 7.b4 later supports it.
57158813525553|f1d3.principle: After each opponent move, check what it left undefended; a free pawn in the centre is worth taking before you continue developing.

5864435021787537|f1c4.headline: Open the centre with 4.d4 against Black's misplaced queen
5864435021787537|f1c4.why: 4.Bc4 develops, but Black catches up with 4...Bb4 5.O-O d6 6.d4 Bg4, pinning your knight, and half of your advantage is gone. Theory explains that 2...Qf6 takes the f6 square from Black's knight and that an early queen gives the opponent chances to develop with tempo; one plan is to open the centre and gain time on the misplaced queen. 3...c6 spent another move on a pawn, so open it now: after 4.d4 exd4 5.Bg5 the bishop develops with tempo on the queen, and after 5...Qd6 6.Nxd4 h6 7.Bh4 Qc7 she has moved again while you have a big lead in development.
5864435021787537|f1c4.principle: When you are ahead in development and the enemy queen is exposed, open the centre at once so your pieces can hit her with tempo.

5915229736017859|c5d4.headline: 4.d4 left e4 hanging: take it with 4...dxe4
5915229736017859|c5d4.why: 4.d4 ignores the attack on e4: the pawn is hit by your d5 pawn and nothing defends it. 4...cxd4 lets White off the hook with 5.e5, closing the centre into a French-style structure where the game is level. 4...dxe4 takes the pawn and hits the knight on f3 at the same time, so White has to retreat with 5.Nfd2, and after 6...cxd4 you are a clean pawn up with a clear advantage.
5915229736017859|c5d4.principle: When your opponent makes a pawn move in the centre, first check what he left undefended: here e4 had no guard, and taking it also attacks a knight.

5925543013863182|e7e5.headline: e5 is covered by the f3 knight: develop with 2...Nf6
5925543013863182|e7e5.why: 2...e5 puts a pawn where the knight on f3 already attacks it and nothing defends it, so 3.Nxe5 simply wins it. 2...Nf6 is the most common master move (44.8%): it develops toward the centre, and Black follows with ...g6, ...Bg7 and castles (5...O-O in the main line) with a level game.
5925543013863182|e7e5.principle: Before pushing a pawn into the centre, count: a square attacked by an enemy knight and defended by none of your pieces is not available yet.

6065829209254937|f1c4.headline: 3...Bb7 hits e4: develop with 4.Bd3, which guards it
6065829209254937|f1c4.why: The bishop on b7 attacks e4, which nothing defends. 4.Bc4 develops but leaves the pawn hanging, so 4...Bxe4 wins it and Black is better. 4.Bd3, played in 94.9% of master games, develops and guards e4 with the same move; after 4...c5 5.c3 Nf6 6.Qe2 d5 7.e5 you gain space with a firm centre and a clear edge. The theory describes the e6b6 setup as aimed at the d5 and e4 squares, so e4 is always the point to check.
6065829209254937|f1c4.principle: Ask what your opponent's last move threatens: the bishop on b7 targets e4, so pick the developing move that also defends it.

6104332673881535|d7d6.headline: Use the Alapin's drawback: 2...Nf6 hits e4 when Nc3 is impossible
6104332673881535|d7d6.why: 2...d6 is too slow against 2.c3: White plays 3.d4 at once, and after 3...Nf6 4.Bd3 cxd4 5.cxd4 has the two-pawn centre the Alapin aims for, with a comfortable edge. 2...Nf6 develops with an attack on e4, and since the c3 square is taken by a pawn, White cannot defend it with a knight. The main line runs 3.e5 Nd5 4.d4 cxd4 5.cxd4, and 5...d6 then starts chipping at White's pawn chain, with equal chances.
6104332673881535|d7d6.principle: Develop with a threat when the opponent's set-up has a hole in its defence: the attacked pawn forces White to react instead of building the centre.

612982152772711|d1b3.headline: Castle first with 7.O-O; 7.Qb3 walks into ...Na5
612982152772711|d1b3.why: 7.Qb3 brings the queen out with two minor pieces still at home, and after 7...Qe7 8.O-O Na5 the knight attacks your queen and bishop together; following 9.Qb5 Nxc4 10.Qxc4 your strong bishop is gone and the game is level. 7.O-O tucks the king away first while the centre is open. After 7...d3 8.e5 Be7 the pawn has pushed Black's bishop back, and only now 9.Qb3 hits f7: after 9...Kf8 10.Bxf7 you win a pawn and Black's king has lost the right to castle.
612982152772711|d1b3.principle: In an open centre, castle before starting queen operations; once your king is safe, the same queen move comes with real threats.

612982152772711|f3g5.headline: Castle first, then hit the d6 bishop with e5
612982152772711|f3g5.why: 7.Ng5 moves the knight a second time with two minor pieces still at home: 7...Ne5 hits your bishop, and after 8.Bb3 h6 9.Nf3 Nxf3+ the knight has walked back and been traded off, and Black is better. 7.O-O gets your king safe and keeps the central play. The bishop on d6 blocks Black's d-pawn, as the theory notes, and stands where your e-pawn can hit it: in the main line 8.e5 drives it to e7, 9.Qb3 lines up with the bishop on c4 against f7, and 10.Bxf7 wins a pawn.
612982152772711|f3g5.principle: A second knight move must win something concrete; when ...Ne5 and ...h6 can simply push it back, castle and use your pawns and pieces in the centre instead.

6230854239967859|c2c3.headline: Break the pin with 5.Be2 before ...Bxf3 costs you d4
6230854239967859|c2c3.why: 4...Bg4 pins your knight and threatens 5...Bxf3, removing the piece that guards d4. 5.c3 adds a pawn defender but leaves the pin in place: in the game line Black plays 5...e5, castles queenside, piles up on d4 and wins it with 8...exd4 9.cxd4 Nxd4. 5.Be2, played in 88.1% of master games, develops and breaks the pin, so a capture on f3 can be answered by a piece instead of ruining your pawns, and 6.Be3 adds another guard to d4.
6230854239967859|c2c3.principle: When a bishop pins your knight to the queen and that knight guards a centre pawn, break the pin by developing a piece in between before the pinner captures.

6251023477722752|c1e3.headline: Bishop to c4 and castle: the book plan against ...Bf5
6251023477722752|c1e3.why: 6.Be3 is not a mistake, but it is off the main path: it develops the queen's bishop before the king's bishop and delays castling, and in the game line your king's bishop then goes to d3 only to be traded off with 7...Bxd3. 6.Bc4 is the most common master move (37%) and the setup the theory gives against ...Bf5 and ...e6, with White standing better: the bishop takes an active diagonal and you castle next with 7.O-O. Then 8.Nh4 goes after the f5 bishop, and after 8...Bg6 9.Nxg6 hxg6 you have the bishop pair.
6251023477722752|c1e3.principle: Develop the kingside pieces first so you can castle: the king's bishop has an obvious active square, while the queen's bishop can wait to see where it is needed.

6280706797964752|c2c3.headline: e4 is attacked twice: add a defender with 4.Qe2
6280706797964752|c2c3.why: After 3...Nf6 the pawn on e4 is attacked by the knight on f6 and the bishop on b7 and defended only by the bishop on d3. 4.c3 adds nothing there: 4...Nxe4 wins it, the knight on e4 is then protected by the bishop on b7, and Black is better. The theory notes say White adds a defender, most often 4.Qe2 (69.3% of masters games), which keeps your pawn and your edge. 4.Nd2 and 4.Nc3 also defend it.
6280706797964752|c2c3.principle: Count attackers and defenders on every pawn your opponent is aiming at; two attackers against one defender means you need a second defender now.

6280706797964752|g1f3.headline: e4 is attacked twice: add a defender with 4.Qe2
6280706797964752|g1f3.why: The bishop on b7 and the knight on f6 both hit e4, and only the bishop on d3 defends it, so 4.Nf3 simply loses the pawn to 4...Nxe4 and Black is better. Theory says White adds a defender here, most often 4.Qe2, 4.Nd2 or 4.f3. 4.Qe2 holds e4 with a second guard, and after 4...e6 5.Nf3 d5 6.e5 you gain space with tempo on the knight and keep a clear edge.
6280706797964752|g1f3.principle: Before a natural developing move, count the attackers and defenders of your centre pawns; if a pawn is attacked twice and defended once, add a defender first.

6309463160940467|e1h1.headline: 6...d6 left f7 weak: hit it twice with 7.Qb3
6309463160940467|e1h1.why: 6...d6 does nothing for f7, which is defended only by the king and already eyed by your bishop on c4. 7.O-O lets Black untangle: 7...Nc6 8.Ng5 Ne5 9.Qb3 Nxc4 swaps off that bishop, and your initiative fades. 7.Qb3 doubles on f7 at once: after 7...Nh6 8.Bxh6 Bxh6 9.Bxf7+ Kf8 you remove the knight that guarded it, take the f7 pawn and leave Black's king stuck on f8, keeping the advantage.
6309463160940467|e1h1.principle: With your bishop already on c4, adding the queen against f7 forces Black to defend it at once, before he can trade off the bishop or castle.

6375481783376729|g1f3.headline: Punish 2...d6 with 3.dxc5 and chase the recapturing queen
6375481783376729|g1f3.why: 3.Nf3 lets Black play 3...cxd4 4.Nxd4 and reach a normal Open Sicilian, and theory notes that trading the c-pawn for your d-pawn was the whole point of 1...c5; most of your edge disappears. By playing 2...d6 instead of 2...cxd4, Black left you the choice, so take first: in the engine line Black regains the pawn with the queen, 3.dxc5 Qa5+ 4.Nc3 Qxc5, and 5.Be3 develops with tempo on her. After 5...Qa5 6.Qd5 Qxd5 7.Nxd5 Kd8 the queens are off and Black's king has lost the right to castle.
6375481783376729|g1f3.principle: When your opponent has to win a pawn back with the queen, develop your pieces with attacks on her and bank the time you gain.

6379793223839|c7c6.headline: Take back with 2...Qxd5; the 2...c6 gambit gives too little
6379793223839|c7c6.why: 2...c6 offers a pawn: after 3.dxc6 Nxc6 4.Nf3 e5 5.Nc3 you have some development for it, but the theory calls the gambit inferior, and White keeps a clear edge. 2...Qxd5, the main line (70.4% of master games), takes back the pawn, which nothing defends. White gains a tempo with 3.Nc3, but your queen steps to a safe square such as d6 (3...Qd6) and you develop normally with ...Nf6 and ...c6. 2...Nf6, the Modern Scandinavian, delays recovering the pawn and is also good.
6379793223839|c7c6.principle: A pawn sacrifice needs concrete compensation; when the pawn you gave can simply be taken back, recover it and develop instead of gambiting a second one.

6545901527067225|d4e5.headline: Develop against the early queen with 4.Nc3; don't trade on e5
6545901527067225|d4e5.why: 4.dxe5 dxe5 releases the central tension for nothing: Black's position frees up, the bishop gets d6 (5...Bd6), and more than half of your advantage is gone. 3...Qf6 brought the queen out early and took the f6 square from Black's knight, so keep developing with 4.Nc3. The queen then becomes a target: 5.Bg5 hits it, and after 5...Qg6 the h-pawn chases it again with 6.h4 and 7.h5.
6545901527067225|d4e5.principle: When the opponent's queen comes out early, keep the position tense and develop pieces that attack it, gaining a tempo each time it must move.

6601544122617741|d2d4.headline: Take the gambit pawn with 3.dxc6; 3.d4 just gives it back
6601544122617741|d2d4.why: After 2...c6 Black threatens 3...cxd5, and 3.d4 does nothing about it: 3...cxd5 restores material and your edge almost disappears. 3.dxc6 accepts the Blackburne gambit, and after 3...Nxc6 you are a clear pawn up. Black's compensation is the faster development the theory describes, so keep developing with 4.Nf3, 5.Nc3 and 6.Bb5 and hold on to the extra pawn.
6601544122617741|d2d4.principle: When a gambit pawn is on offer and you can finish your development afterwards, take it; a half-measure that lets the opponent recapture for free wastes the chance.

666558173554|g5f7.headline: Kick the d4 knight with 6.c3 before any sacrifice on f7
666558173554|g5f7.why: 6.Nxf7 is the Fried Liver idea at the wrong moment: after 6...Kxf7 you are simply a knight for a pawn down, and the knight on d4 covers f3, so your queen has no quick check to follow up. 6.c3, played in 93.8% of master games, hits that knight, which has few squares to retreat to. In the main line 6.c3 b5 7.Bf1 Nxd5 the sacrifice 8.Nxf7 Kxf7 does work, because 9.cxd4 removes the knight and 10.Qf3+ follows with check, and White keeps a small edge.
666558173554|g5f7.principle: A knight in the centre that a pawn can attack is a target: hit it with c3 first, and only sacrifice on f7 once that knight no longer guards f3.

6673250859790786|e7e6.headline: Against 4.Bc4, take the second pawn: 4...cxb2
6673250859790786|e7e6.why: 4.Bc4 leaves your pawn on c3 alive, and 4...e6 lets White take it back with 5.Nxc3, reaching a normal Smith-Morra where White has development for one pawn and you only have a small edge. 4...cxb2 takes a second pawn, and after 5.Bxb2 you are two pawns up with a clear advantage. The theory calls this Danish-style offer too much material for the compensation; follow up with 5...e6, which also blunts the bishop on c4.
6673250859790786|e7e6.principle: Accept a gambit when you can consolidate: here the extra pawns are worth more than White's lead, as long as you blunt the attacking bishop and keep developing.

6730545248551000|c4f7.headline: No sacrifice on f7: prepare d4 with 4.c3
6730545248551000|c4f7.why: 4.Bxf7+ Kxf7 5.Nxe5+ Nxe5 gives a bishop and a knight for two pawns, and the fork 6.d4 does not save it: after 6...Bxd4 7.Qxd4 d6 you are a piece for a pawn down. The real plan in the Giuoco Piano is in the centre: Black controls d4 three times and White only twice. 4.c3, the classical variation (54.9% of masters games), adds a third guard so that White can follow with d4 and build a two-pawn centre.
6730545248551000|c4f7.principle: Before striking in the centre, count who controls the square you want to occupy, and add a pawn to it first; c3 prepares d4 rather than forcing anything early.

6730545248551000|f3e5.why: The pawn on e5 is defended by the knight on c6, so 4.Nxe5 Nxe5 just gives a knight for a pawn, and the knight on e5 then hits your bishop on c4 too. 6730545248551000|f3e5.principle: Before capturing a pawn, count its defenders: one attacker against one defender means you lose the capturing piece for a pawn.

6730545248551000|f3g5.why: 4.Ng5 moves the knight a second time and simply drops it: the queen on d8 sees g5 along the open diagonal, so 4...Qxg5 wins a whole piece. The Giuoco Piano move order, ...Bc5 before ...Nf6, exists precisely to keep that control of g5. 4.c3 is the classical plan instead: it adds control of d4 so your d-pawn can go there, and after 4...Nf6 the quiet 5.d3 holds e4 with a normal game.
6730545248551000|f3g5.principle: A second move with an already developed knight needs a concrete gain; when it wins nothing, bring out a new piece or prepare d4.

6748390364152037|d2d3.headline: The g5 knight is attacked: retreat it with 9.Nf3
6748390364152037|d2d3.why: 8...h6 attacks the knight on g5, and 9.d3 ignores it: 9...hxg5 10.Bxg5 leaves you a knight for a pawn, which is a lost position. Retreat with 9.Nf3, which also attacks the e5 pawn; Black usually gains space with 9...e4, and 10.Ne5 puts the knight on a central square with a balanced game. Masters split almost evenly between 9.Nf3 and 9.Nh3, and both keep the balance.
6748390364152037|d2d3.principle: Before each developing move, check which of your pieces are attacked and undefended; a knight hit by a pawn has to move first.

6756346848148721|d7d5.headline: No early ...d5 in the Sicilian: play 2...d6 and develop
6756346848148721|d7d5.why: 2...d5 opens the centre before you have developed anything, and after 3.exd5 you either leave the pawn or bring your queen out. Leaving it, as in 3...Nf6 4.Bb5+ Bd7 5.Bxd7+ Qxd7 6.c4, White keeps the extra pawn; taking back with 3...Qxd5 lets 4.Nc3 gain time on the queen, and because the c5 pawn blocks the way to a5, she has to go back with 4...Qd8. 2...d6 is the main line (46.1% of masters games): it frees the c8 bishop, defends c5 and controls e5 so ...Nf6 is safe, and after 3.d4 Nf6 4.Nc3 cxd4 5.Nxd4 a6 you have a Najdorf.
6756346848148721|d7d5.principle: Don't open the centre in a way that forces your queen to recapture early; she gets chased and you lose the time you needed for development.

6773809115680684|d1d5.headline: d5 belongs to your knight: put the queen on b3
6773809115680684|d1d5.why: 7.Qd5 hits f7, but 7...Qe7 defends it and your queen has to retreat with 8.Qd3; after 8...Qd8 9.O-O Nf6 you have spent two queen moves for nothing and most of your advantage is gone. 6...h6 spent another move on a pawn, and with Black's pawn on e5 and no c-pawn, d5 is a square no black pawn can ever attack. 7.Qb3 aims at f7 from behind the bishop, Black spends 7...Qe7 defending, and after 8.O-O d6 9.Nd5 the knight takes that square with tempo on the queen, keeping a big advantage.
6773809115680684|d1d5.principle: A central square that enemy pawns can no longer attack is best used by a knight; keep your queen behind the lines and plant the knight there.

6773809115680684|d1e2.headline: Aim queen and bishop at f7 with 7.Qb3
6773809115680684|d1e2.why: 7.Qe2 is too slow: after 7...Nf6 8.O-O Be7 9.Be3 O-O Black has castled, the gambit pawn is just a pawn, and Black is slightly better. 6...h6 spent a move on a pawn while f7 is defended only by the king, and theory stresses how dangerous your c4 bishop is against f7 in the Smith-Morra. 7.Qb3 adds the queen to that pressure, so Black spends 7...Qe7 defending; after 8.O-O d6 9.Nd5 your knight jumps into the hole left by ...e5 with tempo on the queen, and you keep a big advantage.
6773809115680684|d1e2.principle: With your bishop on c4 and the king on e8, add the queen to the pressure on f7: every move Black spends defending it is a move not spent developing.

6773809115680684|e1h1.headline: Punish 6...h6 with 7.Qb3, hitting f7 twice
6773809115680684|e1h1.why: 6...h6 spends a tempo on a pawn move while f7 is still defended only by the king. 7.O-O is natural but lets Black catch up with 7...d6 and 8...Bg4, and most of your advantage slips away. 7.Qb3 lines up the queen with the bishop on c4 against f7, so Black must defend it, and the engine's 7...Qe7 shuts in the bishop on f8; after 9.Nd5 the queen is hit again and you keep a clear advantage.
6773809115680684|e1h1.principle: With the bishop already on c4, adding the queen against f7 forces Black to defend instead of developing, which is how you cash in his lost tempo.

6790604267482997|e2f3.headline: Let the queen take g2: develop with 5.Nf3
6790604267482997|e2f3.why: Black threatens 5...Qxg2, but 5.Bf3 defends it by moving the bishop a second time while two minor pieces are still at home, and after 5...e5 Black catches up in development and most of your advantage is gone. Theory says chasing the g2 pawn is folly and White should be happy to give it up. After 5.Nf3 Qxg2 6.Rg1 Qh3 you have four pieces developed, d4 is coming and the rook on the open g-file can kick the queen again with Rg3, while Black has only the queen out.
6790604267482997|e2f3.principle: When your opponent's queen comes out early, keep developing and let her grab a pawn: every piece you add gains time on her.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3

6820108232337383|f1c4.headline: Against the Petrov, take e5 with 3.Nxe5; 3.Bc4 hangs e4
6820108232337383|f1c4.why: Theory calls 3.Bc4 a beginner's move here: it copies the Italian setup but leaves e4 hanging, and after 3...Nxe4 4.Nxe5 d5 Black has the pawn back and the easier game. 3.Nxe5 is the main line. Black can't recapture at once, since 3...Nxe4 4.Qe2 runs into pins on the e-file (4...Nf6?? 5.Nc6+ wins the queen), so Black first plays 3...d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 and White keeps a small edge.
6820108232337383|f1c4.principle: When both e-pawns are under attack, capture first or defend e4; developing instead lets the opponent take with tempo.

6849990694088956|b2b4.headline: 3...Bc5 leaves e5 loose: take it with 4.Nxe5, not 4.b4
6849990694088956|b2b4.why: 4.b4 hands Black a pawn: after 4...Bxb4 5.Nxe5 O-O 6.Nc4 Re8 Black is castled with a rook bearing down on e4 while your king is still on e1, and Black is clearly better. 4.Nxe5 takes the e5 pawn, which nothing defends, while the knight on c3 still covers e4. Black has to spend moves to regain it, as in 4...Bd4 5.Nf3 Bxc3 6.dxc3 Nxe4 7.Bd3 d5 8.Bxe4 dxe4, and White stays clearly better.
6849990694088956|b2b4.principle: Before reaching for a wing gambit, check what is loose in the centre: an undefended e5 pawn is the simplest gain on the board.

6849990694088956|d2d4.headline: 3...Bc5 left e5 undefended: take it with 4.Nxe5
6849990694088956|d2d4.why: 4.d4 exd4 5.Nxd4 trades off the pawn you could have taken for free, and after 5...O-O Black develops easily and the game is level. 3...Bc5 left e5 attacked once and defended by nothing, so 4.Nxe5 wins it. In the engine line Black hits back with 4...Bd4 5.Nf3 Bxc3 6.dxc3 Nxe4 to regain the pawn, but after 7.Bd3 d5 8.Bxe4 dxe4 White keeps a clear edge.
6849990694088956|d2d4.principle: After every opponent move check what has become loose: when a developing move leaves a centre pawn undefended, take it before following your own plan.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nc3

6849990694088956|f1c4.headline: 3...Bc5 leaves e5 loose: take it with 4.Nxe5
6849990694088956|f1c4.why: The usual replies to 3.Nc3 are 3...Nc6, reaching the Four Knights, or 3...Bb4; 3...Bc5 develops but leaves the e5 pawn undefended. 4.Nxe5 takes it, and in the main line Black gives up the dark-squared bishop to win material back with 4...Bd4 5.Nf3 Bxc3 6.dxc3 Nxe4. 4.Bc4 lets Black cover e5 with 4...d6 5.d3, and the position is level.
6849990694088956|f1c4.principle: Check every developing move by the opponent for what it stopped defending; an undefended centre pawn in front of your knight is often simply free.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nc3

6863144374799225|f3d4.headline: Hit the early queen first: 5.Bg5, then take on d4
6863144374799225|f3d4.why: 5.Nxd4 recaptures at once and lets Black develop calmly with 5...Bb4, so a large part of your advantage disappears. 5.Bg5 develops the bishop with an attack on the queen on f6, so Black has to spend the move on the queen (5...Qd6) instead of playing 5...dxc3, and only then 6.Nxd4 takes the pawn back with your bishop already developed and a big edge. This is the theory's point against 2...Qf6: the queen blocks the knight's best square and hands you developing moves with tempo.
6863144374799225|f3d4.principle: When the opponent's queen sits on an exposed square, look for a developing move that attacks it before you recapture material.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Qf6

6886380190448217|f3d5.headline: Take on d5 with the bishop, with check: 8.Bxd5+
6886380190448217|f3d5.why: d5 is attacked twice and defended by nothing, and 8.Qxd5+ does take the knight, but it brings your queen to the centre with two minor pieces still at home: after 8...Ke8 Black develops with 9...Bd7 and 10...Rd8, and most of your advantage is gone. 8.Bxd5+ wins the same knight with a minor piece and keeps your queen on f3. After 8...Be6 9.Bxc6 bxc6 10.Qxc6 you have won a pawn as well and keep a big advantage.
6886380190448217|f3d5.principle: Capture with a minor piece when you can; taking with the queen puts it in the middle of the board, where Black develops with gain of time.

6994580878022218|b7b6.headline: Settle the centre with 5...cxd4 instead of a slow pawn move
6994580878022218|b7b6.why: 5...b6 develops nothing: White brings out pieces with 6.Nc3 and 7.Be3 while your queenside pawns run forward with 7...c4 and 8...b5, and 9.Ne5 plants a knight on a square both the d4 and f4 pawns support, leaving White better. 5...cxd4 trades your c-pawn for White's d-pawn and opens lines for your pieces: after 6.Nxd4 Nf6 7.Bb5+ Bd7 8.Bxd7+ Qxd7 9.Nc3 Nc6 you are developed with no time lost and slightly better. 5...Nf6 is also fine.
6994580878022218|b7b6.principle: Only make the pawn moves that free your pieces or fight for the centre; here the capture on d4 does both, while ...b6 just costs a tempo.

7050462614834999|c1b2.headline: Step out of the pin with a threat: 9.Qb3 hits b7
7050462614834999|c1b2.why: 9.Bb2 is too slow: Black develops with 9...Nf6, and after 10.h3 Bh5 11.d5 Bxf3 12.Qxf3 Ne5 the knight takes a strong central square and Black has fully equalised. 8...Bg4 pinned your knight to the queen and left b7 without the bishop's protection. 9.Qb3 leaves the pin with a threat on b7, and also lines up with the bishop on c4 against f7. In the main line Black gives up the bishop with 9...Bxf3 10.Qxf3, and you keep the bishop pair and the big centre.
7050462614834999|c1b2.principle: When a bishop pins your knight to the queen, move the queen off the line with a threat, so the pin stops mattering and the opponent has to react.

7062831770535036|c1e3.headline: Push 7.d5 first and keep the b8 knight off c6
7062831770535036|c1e3.why: 7.Be3 lets Black develop with 7...Nc6, and after 8.d5 O-O-O 9.Nf4 Qxd1+ 10.Rxd1 Ne5 the queens are off and Black's knight sits comfortably in the centre, leaving you only a small edge. 7.d5 claims the centre before Black's queenside gets going and takes c6 away from the b8 knight, so it has to go to d7 instead. After 7...Nf6 8.Qd3 Nbd7 9.Be3 O-O-O 10.O-O-O you keep the queens on, more space and a clear advantage.
7062831770535036|c1e3.principle: Before developing, ask where your opponent's next piece wants to go; a pawn move that takes that square away gains space and time at once.

7062831770535036|e1h1.headline: Grab space with 7.d5 before Black sets up ...e6 and ...c6
7062831770535036|e1h1.why: 7.O-O is safe but lets Black build a solid shell with 7...e6 and 9...c6, and your edge shrinks. 7.d5 gains central space at once while Black's queen sits out of play on h5 and his light-squared bishop is already gone: the pawn takes c6 away from Black's knight, which has to go to d7. After 7...Nf6 8.Qd3 Nbd7 9.Be3 both sides castle queenside and you keep a clear edge.
7062831770535036|e1h1.principle: Judge the differences: Black's queen is offside and his light-squared bishop has been traded, so use the moment to take central space he cannot challenge.

7127830528967939|e7e6.headline: Grab space with 3...d4 against the Grob's wing pawns
7127830528967939|e7e6.why: 3...e6 is solid but passive: it shuts in your c8 bishop, and after 4.d4 White's odd first move hardly matters any more and the game is level. 3...d4 takes space instead: in the engine line your pawns follow up with ...e5 and ...e4, driving White's knight back home with 7.Ng1, while 4...h5 makes the advanced g-pawn commit with 5.g5, and Black has a clear advantage. 3...dxc4 is also fine; the theory notes White then has to spend a move on Qa4 to win the pawn back.
7127830528967939|e7e6.principle: When White spends his first moves on wing pawns like g4 and c4, claim the centre with your pawns and use the space to push his pieces back.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. g4/1...d5/2. Bg2/2...c6

7232835087865144|f2f3.headline: Develop with 2.Nf3, attacking e5; 2.f3 only weakens your king
7232835087865144|f2f3.why: The theory calls 2.f3 one of the worst second moves: it defends e4 but takes the f3 square from your knight and weakens your king, and in the line 2...Bc5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Na4 Be7 5.d4 exd4 you end up a pawn down. 2.Nf3, played in 92.2% of master games, develops a piece and attacks the undefended e5 pawn, so Black has to react. It also controls d4 and makes room to castle.
7232835087865144|f2f3.principle: Every opening move should develop a piece or fight for the centre; a pawn move that does neither, and blocks a knight's best square, just hands your opponent time.

741393967202585|e4f5.headline: Castle and let Black release the tension: 5.O-O, not 5.exf5
741393967202585|e4f5.why: 5.exf5 trades your centre pawn for Black's f-pawn: 5...d5 then builds a big centre with tempo on your bishop, and after 6.Bb3 Bxf5 Black has the pawn back with a developed bishop and a slightly better game. The theory calls 4.d3 the best answer to the Rousseau Gambit, leaving Black a difficult position, so keep it that way with 5.O-O: your king is safe and the tension stays. If 5...Bb4 6.c3 fxe4 7.dxe4, you recapture toward the centre, and 8.b4 and 9.a4 gain queenside space with tempo on the bishop, keeping a clear edge.
741393967202585|e4f5.principle: When the opponent's f-pawn is about to open lines, castle first and let them make the exchange, so your king is safe and you recapture toward the centre.

7422621539281278|c1g5.headline: Strike at d6 with 7.Nb5 before ...a6 covers b5
7422621539281278|c1g5.why: 7.Bg5 hits the queen, but 7...Ne7 simply blocks, and after 8.O-O Nbc6 9.Qd2 a6 Black has covered b5 and is ready to castle, so most of your advantage is gone. 6...e6 on top of ...g6 left d6 with no pawn able to cover it and the bishop gone to g7. 7.Nb5 goes straight for that square: after 7...Nf6 8.Nd6+ Ke7 Black's king is stuck in the centre, and 9.e5 Ne8 10.Bg5+ f6 11.exf6+ Bxf6 rips its cover open.
7422621539281278|c1g5.principle: When you are ahead in development and the opponent's position has a hole, attack it at once; one quiet move lets him cover it and castle.

7422621539281278|e1h1.headline: ...g6 plus ...e6 leaves d6 bare: jump in with 7.Nb5
7422621539281278|e1h1.why: 7.O-O gives Black time for 7...a6, which takes b5 away from your knight, and most of your advantage disappears. 6...e6 on top of ...g6 leaves d6 with no pawn able to cover it, and the bishop that should guard it has gone to g7. 7.Nb5 heads straight there: after 7...Nf6 8.Nd6+ Ke7 Black's king is stuck in the centre, and 9.e5 Ne8 10.Bg5+ f6 11.exf6+ Bxf6 tears its cover open.
7422621539281278|e1h1.principle: A square that no enemy pawn can attack is a home for your knight; when Black's pawns leave d6 uncovered, put a knight there with check.

7494602145104629|d2d3.headline: The Elephant Gambit is unsound: take the pawn with 3.exd5
7494602145104629|d2d3.why: 3.d3 turns down the gambit and lets Black open the centre on equal terms: after 3...dxe4 4.Nxe5 Nf6 5.Be2 exd3 6.Nxd3 the material is level and so is the game. The theory notes call 2...d5 unsound and say that taking either pawn wins for White; 3.exd5 is the main move. Black's best try is 3...e4, and 4.Qe2 defends the knight by pinning the pawn, keeping your extra pawn and a clear edge. 3.Nxe5 and 3.d4 are also good.
7494602145104629|d2d3.principle: Take a gambit pawn when you can consolidate; here 4.Qe2 shows you can, so declining with a passive pawn move just hands Black the open game they wanted.

7498080805028408|f3b3.headline: Trade with check, 9.Bxc6+, before Black's knight joins in
7498080805028408|f3b3.why: 9.Qb3 moves the queen a second time with two minor pieces still at home, and Black gains time on it: 9...Nd4 hits the queen, and after 10.Qd3 Bg4 11.h3 Bh5 12.c3 Rd8 Black's rook bears down on your bishop on d5. Your advantage is gone. 9.Bxc6+ removes the knight on c6 with check before it can jump in, breaks Black's pawns with 9...bxc6, and 10.Qh5+ g6 11.Qe2 keeps the king, which can no longer castle, stuck in the centre, and White keeps a large advantage.
7498080805028408|f3b3.principle: When the enemy king is exposed, look at checks and captures first; a forcing trade keeps the initiative, while a quiet queen move hands your opponent time.

7498080805028408|f3f6.headline: Keep the queens on: Black's king is your target
7498080805028408|f3f6.why: Black's king can no longer castle, and your queen is the main piece attacking it. 9.Qxf6 trades it off: after 9...gxf6 10.Bxc6+ bxc6 Black's king is far easier to defend, and your large advantage shrinks to a modest one. 9.Bxc6+ bxc6 10.Qh5+ g6 11.Qe2 keeps the queens on, the king stays in the centre and Black's pawns are split, so your large advantage stays.
7498080805028408|f3f6.principle: Judge the position by its differences: your trump is Black's exposed king, so avoid the queen trade that takes it away and keep the pieces that attack it.

7528031277512488|c1e3.headline: Against 3...Qa5, develop with 6.Bc4 and keep d2 for the bishop
7528031277512488|c1e3.why: 6.Be3 puts the bishop where it can be hit and leaves your c3 knight pinned by the queen on a5; after 6...Bf5 7.Nh4 Nbd7 8.Nxf5 Qxf5 9.Bd3 Qg4 10.Qxg4 Nxg4 the queens are off and the knight attacks your bishop, so you keep little of your edge. Theory describes White's usual set-up as Nf3 and Bc4, with the d2 square freed for the bishop so the c3 knight can later move with tempo on the queen. 6.Bc4, played by masters 65.5% of the time, follows that plan: after 6...Bf5 7.Bd2 the pin is gone and you castle long with 9.O-O-O in the engine line.
7528031277512488|c1e3.principle: Develop each piece to the square the opening's plan gives it, here Bc4 and then Bd2, instead of a square that gives your opponent targets.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qa5

7560471072032627|g1f3.headline: Trade on d5 with 2.exd5 and gain time on the queen
7560471072032627|g1f3.why: Black threatens 2...dxe4, and 2.Nf3 doesn't stop it: the pawn falls with tempo on your knight, and after 3.Ng5 e5 4.h4 h6 5.Nxe4 Be6 Black has a strong centre and the better game. Theory says 2.exd5 is almost always played because trading pawns is in White's interest. When Black recaptures with the queen, 2...Qxd5 3.Nc3 develops with tempo on her, and after 3...Qd8 4.d4 Nf6 5.Nf3 you have the freer development; masters choose 2.exd5 96.9% of the time.
7560471072032627|g1f3.principle: When an exchange forces the enemy queen to recapture in the centre, make it: your pieces then develop with gain of time on her.
