7739923539884250|b7b6.headline: Answer 5.d4 with 5...c4, not the slow 5...b6
7739923539884250|b7b6.why: 5.d4 attacks your c5 pawn and threatens 6.dxc5. 5...b6 spends a move holding it while your king is still on the open e-file: 6.Bb5+ Bd7 7.Qe2+ Be7 8.Nxd5 wins the d5 pawn, because the bishop on d7 cuts your queen off from d5, and White is close to winning. 5...c4 steps out of the attack and keeps everything protected; play continues 6.g3 h6 7.Bg2 Nf6.
7739923539884250|b7b6.principle: With your king still in the centre and the e-file open, don't spend moves on side pawns; every check costs you time or material.

7739923539884250|g8f6.headline: Settle the c5 pawn with 5...c4, then develop
7739923539884250|g8f6.why: 5.d4 threatens 6.dxc5, and with the e-file open your king is short of time. 5...Nf6 is common even among masters, but it lets White develop with pins and checks: 6.Bb5+ Nc6 7.O-O Bg4 8.Bg5, then 10.Re1+, and White gets a clear edge. 5...c4 removes the target first and keeps the balance; the knight still reaches f6 a move later, as in 6.g3 h6 7.Bg2 Nf6.
7739923539884250|g8f6.principle: Before developing, look at your opponent's forcing moves; with the e-file open, every check and pin they get costs you a tempo.

7780638886141553|c2c4.headline: Castle first: 6.O-O guards g2, while 6.c4 drops a pawn
7780638886141553|c2c4.why: The queen on d5 already threatens 6...Qxg2. 6.c4 attacks her, but with your light-squared bishop traded off nothing defends c4, so 6...Qxc4 wins a pawn and Black is clearly better. 6.O-O, played in 96.6% of master games, guards g2 with the king and gets it out of the centre; c4 still comes, as 8.c4 in the main line once 7.Nd2 covers that square.
7780638886141553|c2c4.principle: Black has the lead in development and a queen aimed at your king's side, so castle before starting pawn moves; the theory warns that White easily succumbs here if the centre opens before castling.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Nf6/3. d4/3...Bg4

7832135918552384|d2d3.headline: Black gives you the centre: take it with 2.d4
7832135918552384|d2d3.why: 1...g6 is a hypermodern opening: Black allows White a big centre and hopes to undermine it later. 2.d3 declines the offer, and after 2...c5 3.g3 Nc6 4.Bg2 Bg7 Black has an easy, equal game. 2.d4 (95.1% of masters games) puts a second pawn in the centre while Black has not contested it, gains space and opens the way for your pieces; you keep a small edge.
7832135918552384|d2d3.principle: When the opponent lets you build a two-pawn centre, build it: pawns on e4 and d4 take space and give your pieces room before Black can challenge them.

7908463020324267|b8c6.headline: Hit e4 with 4...Nf6 first so White has no time for c4
7908463020324267|b8c6.why: 4...Nc6 attacks nothing, so White has time for 5.c4, putting pawns on c4 and e4 that clamp the d5 square; after 6.Nc3 g6 7.f3 Black is cramped. 4...Nf6, chosen in 99.5% of master games, hits the e4 pawn first, and White defends it with 5.Nc3, which blocks the c-pawn and rules out an early c4. Then you pick your system, for example 5...a6 as in the taught line.
7908463020324267|b8c6.principle: Develop with a threat: a knight move that attacks e4 makes White spend his move on Nc3 instead of building a pawn clamp on c4 and e4.

7908463020324267|g7g6.headline: Gain time on e4 with 4...Nf6 before anything else
7908463020324267|g7g6.why: 4...g6 is not a blunder, but it puts no pressure on White, who gets to choose a set-up freely: the theory notes say White would love to play 5.c4, the Maróczy bind that makes ...d5 very hard, and in the line 5.Be3 Nf6 6.Nc3 Nc6 7.f3 Bg7 8.Qd2 O-O 9.Bc4 White develops exactly as they like and keeps a small edge. 4...Nf6 (99.5% of masters games) develops and attacks the pawn on e4, so White has no time for 5.c4, which would drop the pawn to 5...Nxe4, and usually defends with 5.Nc3, blocking the c-pawn.
7908463020324267|g7g6.principle: Develop with a threat when you can: a knight move that attacks a pawn forces your opponent to respond and keeps them from setting up the structure they want.

7994400733701852|d7d5.headline: Knight before ...d5: 3...Nc6, then ...Ne5 hits queen and bishop
7994400733701852|d7d5.why: 3...d5 comes too early: after 4.exd5 exd5 the d5 pawn is attacked by the bishop on c4 and the queen on f3 and defended only by your queen, so 5.Qxd5 wins it and threatens mate on f7. The theory says Black should play ...Nc6 before ...d5. 3...Nc6 develops and punishes the early queen: after 4.Ne2 Ne5 the knight hits the queen and the bishop at once, and 5.Qc3 Nxc4 6.Qxc4 gets rid of White's light-squared bishop, leaving Black better.
7994400733701852|d7d5.principle: When White's queen comes out early, develop with threats against it; your pieces gain time while the queen keeps moving.

8013895061699550|d5d6.headline: Keep the extra pawn: develop with 7.Qe2 hitting e5
8013895061699550|d5d6.why: You are a pawn up, and 7.d6 hands it straight back: the pawn on d6 is attacked by the knight on f5, the queen and the c7 pawn and defended by nothing, so 7...Nxd6 wins it, and after 8.Be2 h6 9.Nf3 e4 Black is better. 7.Qe2 develops with a threat against the pawn on e5 and keeps the d5 pawn and a small edge. 7.d4 and 7.O-O are also fine.
8013895061699550|d5d6.principle: When you are ahead in material, prefer a developing move that creates a threat over a pawn push that runs into more attackers than defenders.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...d5/5. exd5/5...Nd4/6. c3

8021519334015813|d2d3.headline: Take the free e5 pawn: 4.Nxe5 is the main line
8021519334015813|d2d3.why: 4.d3 leaves e5 alone and lets the bishop on b4 pin your knight on c3 to the king, which is what the theory says 3...Bb4 was hoping for; after 4...d5 Black takes over the centre and is slightly better. 4.Nxe5, played in 67% of master games, takes the pawn nothing defends, and e4 is safe for now: if 4...Bxc3 5.dxc3 Nxe4, then 6.Qg4 forks the knight on e4 and the g7 pawn. Black usually gets the pawn back later, as in 5.Be2 Re8 6.Nd3 Bxc3 7.dxc3 Nxe4 8.O-O, but you keep the bishop pair and a small edge.
8021519334015813|d2d3.principle: Count before you capture: e5 has no defender and the knight on c3 covers e4, so the pawn is free unless Black can remove that defender safely.

8021519334015813|d2d4.headline: Take 4.Nxe5 first; 4.d4 pins your own knight and drops e4
8021519334015813|d2d4.why: As the theory says, 3...Bb4 threatens to pin your knight as soon as the d-pawn moves. 4.d4 does exactly that, so the knight on c3 can no longer take back on e4: 4...Nxe4 grabs the pawn, and after 5.Qd3 d5 6.dxe5 O-O 7.a3 Bxc3+ 8.bxc3 Re8 Black is better. 4.Nxe5, the main move (67% of master games), takes the free pawn while e4 is still covered; if 4...Bxc3 5.dxc3 Nxe4, then 6.Qg4 forks the knight on e4 and the g7 pawn. Black usually regains the pawn with 4...O-O and 7...Nxe4, but White keeps a small edge.
8021519334015813|d2d4.principle: Before moving the d-pawn, look at the bishop on b4: once d2 is empty your knight on c3 is pinned to the king and stops defending e4.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nc3/3...Bb4

8144277447096351|f1c4.headline: Black gave up the c8 bishop: hit b7 with 6.Qb3
8144277447096351|f1c4.why: 6.Bc4 lets Black answer 6...Qf6, and after 7.Qb3 Nd7 8.Qxb7 Rb8 9.Qa6 Qxa6 10.Bxa6 the queens come off and Black's pieces get active, so you keep less of your edge. Theory calls 3...Bg4 dubious, and after 4...Bxf3 Black no longer has the light-squared bishop that guards b7. 6.Qb3 attacks the pawn on b7 at once, before Black's queen can help, and after 6...Nd7 7.Be3 Bc5 8.Bxc5 Nxc5 9.Qb5+ Nd7 10.Qxb7 you win the pawn with queens still on.
8144277447096351|f1c4.principle: When your opponent trades off a bishop, the squares it guarded become weak; aim your pieces at them, here the light squares b7 and f7.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...Bg4

8186436489067117|b5e2.headline: Keep the bishop on b5 and free the other with 8.d3
8186436489067117|b5e2.why: 8.Be2 retreats the bishop a second time with two minor pieces still at home, and Black gains time on your knight: after 8...h6 9.Nh3 Bxh3 10.gxh3 Qc8 11.d3 Qxh3 your kingside pawns are wrecked, the extra pawn is gone and Black is clearly better. 8.d3 leaves the bishop on b5 pinning the c6 knight and opens the diagonal for your c1 bishop. After 8...Qd5 9.Bxc6+ Qxc6 10.O-O Bd6 11.Qf3 you have castled and kept the extra pawn.
8186436489067117|b5e2.principle: Instead of retreating a piece that is doing a job, make the move that brings a new piece into play.

826798325202564|c2c3.headline: Take back with 4.Nxd4: that is why 3.Nf3 came first
826798325202564|c2c3.why: 3.Nf3 is the Morphy gambit, and 3...e6 does nothing to keep the pawn: d4 is attacked twice and defended by nothing. 4.c3 offers a second pawn instead of collecting the first, and after 4...dxc3 5.Nxc3 you are a pawn down with Black slightly better. 3.Nf3 was played to recapture with the knight rather than the queen, which Black would hit with ...Nc6, so 4.Nxd4 (99.7% of masters games) wins the pawn back and reaches a normal Open Sicilian with a small edge for White.
826798325202564|c2c3.principle: 3.Nf3 offered d4 as a gambit; once Black declines to secure the pawn, take it back with the piece you prepared and keep your share of the centre.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. Nf3

8292354532353769|f3e5.headline: The e5 pawn is poisoned: trade knights with 4.Nxd4
8292354532353769|f3e5.why: 4.Nxe5 falls into the trap: 4...Qg5 attacks the knight on e5 and the pawn on g2 at once, and after 5.O-O Qxe5 you have lost a knight for a pawn. Theory calls 3...Nd4 a one-trick pony: Black moved the knight a second time to tempt you into taking e5, and as long as you avoid that you are comfortably ahead. 4.Nxd4 exd4 trades the knights and dislodges Black's pawn from e5, and after 5.O-O Nf6 6.Re1 d6 7.c3 Be7 8.cxd4 you win a pawn with a lead in development.
8292354532353769|f3e5.principle: When your opponent moves the same knight twice to bait you, don't take the bait: trade the knight off and the time he spent on it is simply lost.

8308599203837326|e4f5.headline: Meet the Rousseau Gambit with 4.d4, not 4.exf5
8308599203837326|e4f5.why: Black threatens 4...fxe4, but 4.exf5 lets Black kick your knight with 4...e4, and after 5.Nd4 Nf6 most of your advantage is gone; theory calls the capture a common beginners' mistake. 3...f5 loosens Black's centre, so hit it: after 4.d4 fxe4 5.Nxe5 you are in an improved version of the Latvian Gambit main line, and after 4...exd4 5.e5 the centre opens and you castle quickly with a big initiative.
8308599203837326|e4f5.principle: When your opponent loosens his centre with an early flank pawn move, strike in the centre with your own pawn instead of grabbing the flank pawn he offers.

8342193165505706|d7d6.headline: Save the d-pawn for ...d5: play 4...a6, not 4...d6
8342193165505706|d7d6.why: The theory's answer to 2.Bc4 is ...e6 followed by ...d5, which hits the bishop and gives Black a free centre, as in 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.O-O d5. 4...d6 parks the d-pawn one square short, and after 5.d4 cxd4 6.Nxd4 Nf6 7.Be3 White has a comfortable Open Sicilian and a small edge. 4...a6, the most common master move (49.3%), keeps the d-pawn free to go to d5 and takes b5 away from White's knight and bishop; after 5.d4 cxd4 6.Nxd4 Qc7 the game is close to level. 4...Nf6 is also good.
8342193165505706|d7d6.principle: Make each pawn move count: the d-pawn belongs on d5, where it hits the bishop on c4 and frees your pieces, so don't spend a tempo putting it on d6.

8378513320650736|e1h1.headline: e4 is hit twice: add a defender with 5.Qe2
8378513320650736|e1h1.why: After 4...Nf6, e4 is attacked twice, by the bishop on b7 and the knight on f6, and defended only by the bishop on d3. 5.O-O ignores this and 5...Nxe4 wins a pawn. 5.Qe2, the most common master move (62.6%), adds a second defender; after 5...d5 6.e5 Nfd7 7.c3 you have a French-style space advantage and a clear edge. 5.Nbd2 also defends, and 5.e5 kicks the knight away.
8378513320650736|e1h1.principle: Each time your opponent adds an attacker to a pawn, count again: two attackers against one defender means you must add a defender or move the pawn before doing anything else.

8399621132422899|e2e3.headline: Start with a centre pawn: 1.e4 claims the centre
8399621132422899|e2e3.why: 1.e3 is not a mistake, but the theory calls it passive: it lets Black take over the centre with ...e5 and ...d5, and the pawn on e3 shuts in your queenside bishop, so White's first-move edge is gone. 1.e4 puts a pawn in the centre, opens lines for the queen and the king's bishop, and keeps a black pawn off e4, so your knight can go to f3 without being kicked. It is the most popular first move at every level (45.5% of master games); 1.d4, 1.Nf3 and 1.c4 are good too.
8399621132422899|e2e3.principle: The opening is a race for development and control of the centre, so the first move should put a pawn on a central square and open lines for your pieces.

8432999302569785|c2c3.headline: Recapture 4.Nxd4: open lines are what you get for the pawn
8432999302569785|c2c3.why: The pawn on d4 is attacked twice and defended only by the knight on c6. The theory notes call 4.c3 a playable gambit that turns into a Smith-Morra, but after 4...dxc3 5.Nxc3 e6 6.Be2 d6 you are a pawn down and Black is already slightly better. 4.Nxd4 (99.8% of masters games) wins the pawn back and gives you open lines for your bishops in return for Black's extra centre pawn.
8432999302569785|c2c3.principle: In the Open Sicilian, White trades a centre pawn for open lines and fast development; recapture on d4 so that trade happens on equal material instead of a pawn down.

8432999302569785|f1c4.headline: You played 3.Nf3 to recapture: do it now with 4.Nxd4
8432999302569785|f1c4.why: The point of 3.Nf3 is to take back on d4 with the knight and reach a normal Open Sicilian. 4.Nxd4 does exactly that, and masters choose it 99.8% of the time. 4.Bc4 leaves Black the extra pawn and time to hit back in the centre with 4...Nf6 5.Qe2 d5, and Black is the one who ends up better.
8432999302569785|f1c4.principle: Recapturing in the centre with a piece keeps your central presence; leaving the pawn hands the opponent both material and central play.

843339252523142|d2d4.headline: Kick the b4 knight before opening the centre: 10.a3
843339252523142|d2d4.why: 10.d4 gives Black time to untangle: 10...Qf6 offers a queen trade, and after 11.Qe2 Kd7 the king walks to safety on c7, your attack is gone and Black is the one with the edge. 10.a3 attacks the knight on b4 first, and after 10...Na6 it no longer protects d5. Then 11.Nxd5 cxd5 12.d4 opens the centre while Black's king is still on e6, and 12...e4 13.Qxe4+ wins a pawn with check.
843339252523142|d2d4.principle: In the Fried Liver your compensation is the exposed king, and it fades if you give it time; remove its defenders first, then open lines while the king is still in the centre.

843339252523142|e1h1.headline: Keep the initiative: 10.a3 kicks the b4 knight before castling
843339252523142|e1h1.why: You are a piece for a pawn down, so every move must keep the pressure on the king on e6. 10.O-O lets Black regroup: 10...Qf6 offers a queen trade, 11.Qd1 avoids it, and after 11...Kd7 the king heads for safety and the extra piece starts to tell. 10.a3 hits the knight on b4, which retreats to a6, out of play; then 11.Nxd5 cxd5 12.d4 opens lines against the king, and after 12...e4 13.Qxe4+ you have won a pawn back with check, the king is still exposed, and White keeps an edge.
843339252523142|e1h1.principle: After a sacrifice you have to keep attacking: make moves that create threats against the king or its defenders, or the extra piece decides the game.

8455496353401048|c1g5.headline: 6...Nf6 leaves f7 weak: 7.Ng5 hits it with knight and bishop
8455496353401048|c1g5.why: 7.Bg5 is natural development, but it lets Black play 7...Be7 and 8...O-O, and your gambit compensation is gone: Black is slightly better. After 6...Nf6 the f7 square is defended only by the king, and 7.Ng5 lines up the knight with the bishop on c4 against it. Black has to block the bishop with 7...d5, and 8.Nxd5 wins that pawn with a large advantage.
8455496353401048|c1g5.principle: While the opponent's king is still on e8, f7 is guarded only by the king; when a knight can join your c4 bishop against it, look at that first.

8471347538789945|c2c3.headline: 3.c3 doesn't defend e4: develop the bishop to d3
8471347538789945|c2c3.why: 2...Bb7 attacks e4, and 3.c3 is a pawn move that neither develops nor defends it: 3...Bxe4 wins the pawn, and after 4.c4 e6 5.Nc3 Bb7 you have spent two moves on the c-pawn and Black is better. 3.Bd3, the main move (68.7% of masters games), defends e4 and develops a piece at the same time, keeping your edge. 3.Nc3 and 3.Nd2 also defend the pawn.
8471347538789945|c2c3.principle: In the opening, make the pawn moves that free your pieces or hold the centre; a support move like c3 is pointless when a developing move can defend the pawn under attack.

8471347538789945|g1f3.headline: 2...Bb7 attacks e4: defend it with 3.Bd3 before anything else
8471347538789945|g1f3.why: The bishop on b7 hits e4 and nothing defends that pawn, so 3.Nf3 simply drops it to 3...Bxe4 and your clear edge turns into a worse position. 3.Bd3 is the main move (68.7% of masters games): it develops a piece and defends e4 at the same time, so you keep the two-pawn centre and your edge. 3.Nc3 and 3.Nd2 also defend the pawn.
8471347538789945|g1f3.principle: When the opponent's last move creates a threat, stop it first, ideally with a developing move, and only then continue your own plan.

853185718049302|d4e5.headline: Keep the tension and develop: 5.Be3, not 5.dxe5
853185718049302|d4e5.why: 5.dxe5 dxe5 releases the tension on Black's terms: the e5 pawn is solid again, Black's bishop gets d6 (6...Bd6), and most of your advantage is gone. Black has made only pawn moves and a queen move, so keep adding pieces with 5.Be3. In the main line 5...Nc6 6.Nc3 Bg4 7.d5 drives the knight back with 7...Nb8, and 8.Nb5 followed by 9.Nxa7 wins a pawn.
853185718049302|d4e5.principle: When the opponent has spent the opening on pawn moves and an early queen, keep developing and let the central tension work for you instead of trading it off.

8567362508613525|d2d4.headline: Push 6.a4 to chase the b6 bishop; 6.d4 drops a pawn
8567362508613525|d2d4.why: 6.d4 opens the centre too early: after 6...exd4 White does not get the pawn back, the refutation goes 7.Qb3 Qe7 8.O-O, and Black ends up better. 6.a4 uses the pawns you have already pushed: it threatens a5 to trap the bishop on b6, the plan the theory gives against this decline, so Black spends time on 6...a6 and 8...Ba7 while you castle and play 8.d3, keeping a slight edge.
8567362508613525|d2d4.principle: Your pawns on b4 and c3 already give you queenside space, so play on that wing with a4-a5 against the bishop on b6 instead of opening the centre for Black's pieces.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4/4...Bb6

8645343577179290|g7g6.headline: Shut the c4 bishop's diagonal with 7...e6 before e5 opens lines
8645343577179290|g7g6.why: 7...g6 leaves the bishop on c4 aiming straight at f7, and after 8.Nxc6 bxc6 9.e5 Ng4 10.Re1 d5 11.Nxd5 cxd5 12.Bxd5 the centre blows open around your uncastled king and White is clearly better. Theory notes that against the Sozin bishop Black almost always answers with ...e6, closing its diagonal toward f7. With 7...e6 the bishop bites on a pawn, and after 8.Nxc6 bxc6 9.Re1 e5 White has to retreat it with 10.Bf1, and the game stays roughly level.
8645343577179290|g7g6.principle: With your king still in the centre and a bishop aimed at f7, block that diagonal before you spend time on a kingside fianchetto.

8673706909167185|c1a3.headline: Castle and open lines: 8.O-O, then e5 and Rd1
8673706909167185|c1a3.why: 8.Ba3 does nothing about the d4 pawn: 8...dxc3 opens the position for Black, and after 9.O-O Nge7 10.Bxe7 Qxe7 11.Nxc3 your bishop has been traded off and Black is clearly better. 8.O-O, the only move in the 63 master games, gets the king safe and brings the rook toward the centre. In the main line 8...d3 9.e5 drives the queen away with tempo, and after 10.Rd1 Nge7 11.Bxd3 you win back a pawn, with 12.Ba3 still to come.
8673706909167185|c1a3.principle: In the Evans your pawns buy a lead in development: castle and open lines with e5 and the rook on the d-file before Black can untangle.

8692601699406729|d7d5.headline: Don't open the centre behind in development: play 5...Qc7
8692601699406729|d7d5.why: 5...d5 opens the position while White has more pieces out: after 6.exd5 exd5 the d5 pawn is attacked by the c3 knight, 7.Bb5 pins the knight on c6, and once 7...Bd7 blocks the queen's defence of d5, 8.Nxd5 wins the pawn. 5...Qc7 is the main move (65.6% of master games): the queen takes a safe square with good scope, and Black develops the queenside first with ...a6, ...b5 and ...Bb7, keeping a normal Sicilian.
8692601699406729|d7d5.principle: When the opponent has more pieces developed, keep the centre closed and finish developing before you play the freeing pawn break.

8692601699406729|g8e7.headline: Keep d6 covered: 5...Qc7, not a knight that blocks your bishop
8692601699406729|g8e7.why: 5...Nge7 shuts in the f8 bishop, the only piece guarding the hole on d6 that 2...e6 left, so 6.Ndb5 threatens mate on d6. After 6...Ng6 7.Nd6+ Bxd6 8.Qxd6 Qe7 9.Qxe7+ Kxe7 you have lost the bishop pair and the right to castle, and White is clearly better. 5...Qc7, the Bastrikov, puts the queen on a safe square with good scope where it also watches d6, and Black continues with queenside development, ...a6 and ...b5, as in 6.Be3 a6 7.Qf3 b5; masters choose it 65.6% of the time.
8692601699406729|g8e7.principle: In the ...e6 Sicilians, know that d6 is the square White's knights want, and develop so that it stays covered rather than blocking the bishop that guards it.

8698679373330427|c8f5.headline: 3.Bf4 leaves c4 hanging: take it with 3...dxc4
8698679373330427|c8f5.why: After 3...Bf5 4.Nc3 Qb6 5.Qd2 Nf6 6.f3 h6 7.e3 e6 8.g4 White gains kingside space and chases your bishop, and the edge passes to White. 3.Bf4 develops a piece but leaves c4 behind: the c4 pawn is attacked once and not defended at all, with the f1 bishop still shut in by the e2 pawn. 3...dxc4 wins it, and after 4.g3 Nf6 5.Nf3 Nd5 6.Bd2 b5 your queenside pawns hold the extra pawn; masters take on c4 45.2% of the time.
8698679373330427|c8f5.principle: When your opponent leaves a pawn en prise and you can support it afterwards, take it: in the Slav the c6 pawn already backs up ...b5.

8716466597702343|b1c3.headline: Take the gambit pawn: 3.dxe6 keeps you a pawn up
8716466597702343|b1c3.why: 2...e6 hits your d5 pawn, and 3.Nc3 lets Black recapture with 3...exd5: material is level again and so is the game. 3.dxe6 removes the attacker and takes a second pawn; after 3...Bxe6 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.d4 you are a clean pawn up with normal development. The theory rates 2...e6 an inferior gambit that does not give enough for the pawn.
8716466597702343|b1c3.principle: Accept a gambit when you can develop normally afterwards: here Nf3 and d4 come easily, so take on e6 and keep the extra pawn.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5

8716466597702343|d2d4.headline: Take the gambit pawn with 3.dxe6: 2...e6 gives too little
8716466597702343|d2d4.why: Black threatens 3...exd5 to win the pawn back, and 3.d4 does nothing about it: after 3.d4 exd5 you reach a symmetrical, quiet position where queens can come off with 6.Qe2+ Qe7 7.Qxe7+ Kxe7, and most of your advantage is gone. Theory lists 2...e6 among the Scandinavian gambits that are inferior and don't give enough for the pawn. 3.dxe6 Bxe6 simply keeps the extra pawn, and after 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.d4 you are developed and a clean pawn up.
8716466597702343|d2d4.principle: When an unsound gambit offers you a pawn that you can keep without danger, take it and develop; giving it back only hands your opponent the equality he gambled for.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5

8751595729469873|c1a3.headline: Hit the queen first: 9.e5 gains time before 10.Nxc3
8751595729469873|c1a3.why: 9.Ba3 aims at e7 to keep Black's king in the centre, but 9...Nge7 blocks the diagonal, and after 10.Bxe7 Qxe7 11.Nxc3 O-O Black has castled and keeps his extra pawns with the better game. 9.e5 attacks the queen on f6 first, so after 9...Qg6 you recapture with 10.Nxc3 having gained a tempo, and your e5 pawn takes f6 away from Black's knight, which has to develop with 10...Nge7; White keeps a small edge.
8751595729469873|c1a3.principle: Develop with threats: a pawn move that hits the queen lets you win back material with gain of time, while a quiet bishop move gives Black the time to block and castle.

8849788781204745|g7g6.headline: Don't open the long diagonal: 7...g6 loses the h8 rook
8849788781204745|g7g6.why: Your g7 pawn is the only thing between the queen on d4 and the rook on h8. 7...g6 opens that diagonal and 8.Qxh8 wins the rook, which decides the game. 7...Nf6, the usual move (82.2% of master games), develops and keeps the diagonal shut; after 8.Bg5 e6 you follow with ...Be7 and castle, with a normal, roughly level game.
8849788781204745|g7g6.principle: Before each pawn move, look at the captures it allows: moving the g-pawn here opens the d4-h8 diagonal straight to an undefended rook.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Qxd4

8877803564094104|d2d3.headline: Stop ...Ng4 with 6.h3: the Stafford aims at f2
8877803564094104|d2d3.why: In the Stafford, Black gives up a pawn to open lines for the bishop on c5 and a knight jump to g4, both aimed at f2. 6.d3 develops but doesn't stop it: 6...Ng4 7.Be3 Nxe3 8.fxe3 Bxe3 wins the pawn back and plants the bishop deep in your camp, leaving Black better. 6.h3 takes g4 away first, and after 6...Qd4 7.Qf3 Qe5 8.d3 you keep the extra pawn in a sound position.
8877803564094104|d2d3.principle: Ask what your opponent's gambit is aiming at and take that square away first, as h3 does against ...Ng4, then develop.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5

8877803564094104|d2d4.headline: 6.h3 stops ...Ng4 and keeps your extra pawn
8877803564094104|d2d4.why: Black's bishop on c5 already aims at f2, and 6...Ng4 would add the knight and win a pawn. 6.d4 hits the bishop, but it simply takes, 6...Bxd4, and Black has his pawn back with a level game. 6.h3 takes g4 away from the knight and you stay a pawn up; Black's queen comes out with 6...Qd4 7.Qf3 Qe5, but after 8.d3 Bd4 9.Nd1 the queens come off with 10...Qxg3 and you keep the extra pawn.
8877803564094104|d2d4.principle: Ask what your opponent wants: here everything Black has aims at ...Ng4 and f2, so one small pawn move that takes g4 away keeps the pawn you won.

956431266193433|d2d3.headline: Hit the e5 queen with 5.Nf3 instead of a pawn move
956431266193433|d2d3.why: 5.d3 is a quiet pawn move that lets Black catch up: 5...Bg4 6.Be3 Bxe2 7.Qxe2 Nf6 and your edge is gone. As the theory notes say, the early queen check achieves little and the queen will have to move again. 5.Nf3 develops the knight toward the centre and attacks the queen on e5; after 5...Qd6 6.d4 e6 7.Nb5 Qd8 she has been driven all the way home while you developed, and you keep a clear edge.
956431266193433|d2d3.principle: When the opponent's queen comes out early, develop with moves that attack it; every tempo she spends running is a developing move you gain.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3

961430540554751|c1e3.headline: Ask the g4 bishop at once: 6.h3 before Black develops
961430540554751|c1e3.why: 6.Be3 gives Black time for 6...Nf6, and when h3 comes a move later the bishop escapes with 7...Bh5 8.g4 Bg6, exactly the retreat route the theory describes, and White's edge shrinks. 6.h3, played in 84.2% of master games, hits the bishop on g4 while it still has to decide: 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3 gives you the bishop pair and an active queen, then 8.Bd2 unpins the knight on c3 and 9.O-O-O follows.
961430540554751|c1e3.principle: A bishop that pawns can attack is a target: kick it with the h-pawn right away, before Black's development lets it retreat to a safe square for free.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qa5

961430540554751|f1e2.headline: Question the g4 bishop with 6.h3 and take the bishop pair
961430540554751|f1e2.why: 6.Be2 is passive: Black continues 6...Nd7 and trades off the light-squared bishop with 7...Bxe2, and half of your advantage is gone. 6.h3, the choice in 84.2% of master games, puts the question to the bishop at once. After 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3 you have the bishop pair and an active queen, and 8.Bd2 and 9.O-O-O follow; if the bishop retreats instead, the theory notes it gets chased to g6.
961430540554751|f1e2.principle: Create imbalances that favour you: forcing the bishop to take on f3 gives you the bishop pair in an open position, while a passive bishop move lets Black swap off a piece cheaply.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qa5

972282943199495|g1f3.headline: 3...d6 declines the gambit: take back with 4.cxd4
972282943199495|g1f3.why: With 3...d6 Black declines the Smith-Morra, and the pawn on d4 is attacked twice and defended by nothing. 4.Nf3 lets Black accept after all: after 4...dxc3 5.Nxc3 you are a pawn down in a gambit with no edge left. 4.cxd4 (98.7% of masters games) wins the pawn back and gives you the ideal two-pawn centre with pawns on e4 and d4, and a clear edge.
972282943199495|g1f3.principle: When your opponent declines your gambit, recover the pawn and take the centre; do not keep offering material you no longer need to give.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3

977859217629606|e4e5.headline: Guard e4 with 11.Re1; 11.e5 runs into ...d6
977859217629606|e4e5.why: 10...Nf6 hits your e4 pawn, but 11.e5 overreaches: 11...d6 attacks your queen on c5 and the e5 pawn together, and after 12.Qb5 a6 13.Qb3 dxe5 Black has won the pawn and most of your advantage is gone. 11.Re1 defends e4 by bringing the rook to the e-file, where Black's king still stands on e8. After 11...d6 12.Qb5 Bd7 13.Qb3 Qe7 14.Nxc3 you pick up the c3 pawn while developing and keep a clear advantage.
977859217629606|e4e5.principle: Before pushing a pawn, check whether a counter-push can hit it and a loose piece of yours at once; here your queen on c5 makes ...d6 a double attack.

983258444083142|b1c3.headline: Kick the f6 knight with 7.e5 and gain time
983258444083142|b1c3.why: 7.Nc3 is a natural developing move, but it gives Black time for 7...d6 and ...Be7, and more than half of your advantage slips away. 6...Nf6 put the knight where your e-pawn can hit it: 7.e5 gains space with tempo, and in the main line the knight retreats with 7...Nh7, the poor square that ...h6 made available. Then 8.Nc3 and 9.Ne4 bring your knight to 10.Nd6+, and after 10...Bxd6 11.Qxd6 your queen sits deep in Black's camp while the king is still in the centre.
983258444083142|b1c3.principle: When an enemy piece can be attacked by a pawn or piece that also improves your position, do that first, so the opponent spends the move retreating instead of developing.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...h6
